title: Y2K
review:
At the turn of the millennium, the world braced for apocalypse-by-software. Computers were supposed to crash, planes fall, nukes launch — all because our calendars ticked over from ’99 to ’00. Y2K taps into that unique flavor of late-90s hysteria, remixing it into a neon-soaked, teen-disaster-comedy where the floppy disk is deadlier than the knife. For anyone who lived through the glitch panic — or grew up hearing about it — the movie scratches that nostalgic itch while winking at our modern tech obsession.

This isn’t high cinema — it’s glitch-core absurdity that embraces its own stupidity. The plot doesn’t matter as much as the aesthetic: frosted tips, AOL dial-up tones, rave sequences, and a VHS-colored sense of dread. It’s Final Destination meets Not Another Teen Movie, coded in HTML. And somehow… it works. The characters are charming, the deaths are hilarious, and the sheer commitment to the bit is admirable. If you’re in on the joke, you’ll have a blast. If not, you’ll still appreciate the microwave kill.

title: Red One
review:
Holiday movies always get a pass — we watch them less for quality and more for the vibe. Red One tries to be the new go-to Christmas blockbuster, throwing big-name actors, over-the-top action, and even a CGI polar bear into the mix. In a world where holiday movies are still printing money, it makes sense this one exists.

That said, it’s dumb. Like, really dumb. The kind of movie where you sit there going, “Who greenlit this?” but still laugh once or twice because the cast is too good not to be entertaining. We watched it at Christmas, which definitely helped. As a holiday flick on in the background while you’re wrapping gifts or eating leftovers — it works. But beyond that? Straight-up garbage.

title: Gladiator II
review:
This sequel came swinging with an oversized budget, star power, and a promise to bring back the blood-and-sand spectacle. On paper, it’s prestige cinema — high art action with an Oscar-friendly cast, trying to revive the ancient epic for a new generation. But in practice, it felt more like spectacle for spectacle’s sake. The fighting was brutal, the animals were insane, and it delivered some gnarly set pieces, but the story didn’t stick.

For the Heart, it was entertaining enough — a big, bloody, expensive flick that looked good on the big screen, even if it didn’t leave much after. But for the Brain? The whole thing felt hollow. Strip away the two (okay, maybe three) marquee actors, and what’s left? Not much. A lot of noise, a lot of blood, and a lot of moments that should’ve hit harder than they did.

title: The Fire Inside
review:
Sports dramas always have a place — they tap into grit, struggle, and triumph, even when we know exactly where the story is going. The Fire Inside shines a light on women’s boxing, specifically Olympic women’s boxing, which rarely gets this kind of cinematic treatment. That alone makes it worth paying attention to, giving representation to a world that’s too often overlooked.

It was inspirational, well-told, and moving in the moment. Seeing a story you don’t usually get to see was refreshing, and even though boxing isn’t the most popular sport, this felt like a good entry point. Not life-changing, not unforgettable, but a solid, uplifting movie worth a watch.

At the same time, it’s predictable. You know what’s going to happen the second you press play, and it doesn’t really surprise you. Still, there’s something to be said for a familiar story told with sincerity. If you’re into sports dramas, especially boxing, it’s worth it. If not, skip it.

title: Anora
review:
Sad, raw, and kind of twisted — this one plays like a slice-of-life fairytale gone off the rails. A stripper, a rich Russian kid, and a whirlwind that feels equal parts fantasy and nightmare.

It’s layered, heartfelt, and visually fun to watch, but the ending leaves you sitting there like… damn. Entertaining, award-worthy, and definitely not dull — but also messed up enough that you’ll question what you just watched.

title: Baby Girl
review:
From the first scene, this one felt weird as hell — like, “why am I watching this with nachos in my lap and a full theater breathing next to me” weird. It’s explicit, awkward, and almost plays like softcore wrapped up as “art cinema.” The whole time you’re asking: did Nicole Kidman want this, or did the director just want to see Nicole Kidman do this?

It’s trippy, erotic, slice-of-life chaos — entertaining in its own bizarre way, but also the kind of movie you squirm through and then can’t stop talking about later. Maybe that’s the point: to be so strange and uncomfortable that it becomes iconic just by existing.

title: Better Man
review:
Better Man is one of those just-makes-you-feel movies. I first caught it at AMC Unseen, but I rewatched it today just to put this review together — and it still hit just as hard. It’s a love story to oneself, a love story to life. Robbie Williams made this biopic about his journey, and it’s powerful, raw, and really well done. The CGI was surprisingly strong, the money on screen shows, and it felt like a true passion project.

What stood out most was how fresh and original it felt. It didn’t play like a typical musical or biopic. It was captivating, magical, even mystic at times — and crazy how many details were so spot-on they added to the weight of the story. The drug use was portrayed with such raw honesty it became one of the hardest but most powerful parts of the film. It’s a rollercoaster, emotional and surreal, but always compelling.

Yes, there are strange choices — the monkey bit is a hurdle to get past — but once you’re through it, the movie finds its rhythm. The songs, the performances, and the emotional payoff at the end make it more than worth it. Even if you’re not familiar with Robbie’s career, the movie captures his rise to fame and the toll it took in a way that’s both heartfelt and cinematic.

title: The Last Showgirl
review:
A slice-of-life story that peels back the glitter of Las Vegas to show what happens when the show’s over — literally. Once a star of the iconic showgirl scene, an aging performer is forced to reckon with a world that’s moved on, a family that’s complicated, and a self-image caught between denial and survival.

It’s a sad, heavy, and at times depressing watch, but that’s the point: the performances dig deep, the characters are messy, and the story lingers in the uncomfortable reality of aging out in an industry built on youth. Jamie Lee Curtis shines, reminding us that great acting isn’t always glamorous — sometimes it’s raw, layered, and devastating.

title: Den of Thieves 2: Pantera
review:

It’s the kind of movie you throw on with your dad or when you don’t want to think too hard. Nothing remarkable, nothing offensive — just serviceable popcorn entertainment that fills two hours without asking much from you. It doesn’t do anything new or surprising, but it isn’t bad enough to switch off either. You’ll sit through it, enjoy a few moments, and then immediately forget about it. For fans who live in this genre, it scratches the itch. For everyone else, it’s disposable background noise.

title: One of Them Days
review:

A Friday night, Saturday night, Tuesday afternoon kind of movie — whenever you need to laugh and just vibe out.

title: The Substance
review:
Body horror with brains — The Substance takes one of the most universal fears (getting older) and drags it to the surface in grotesque, stylish fashion. It’s not just gore for the sake of shock, it’s a cinematic war between self-image and a society obsessed with youth.

For us, it was tense, uncomfortable, and at times really hard to watch. The movie builds suffocating dread scene by scene, and the commentary hits close to home. That said, the ending dragged on way too long and killed some of the momentum. Still, up until that stretch, it was sharp, layered, and disturbingly entertaining.

title: Talk to Me
review:
Talk to Me is part of the new wave of A24 horror that knows how to be both terrifying and smart. It’s not just jump scares — it’s layered with grief, teen chaos, and the kind of imagery that sticks in your head long after the credits. Seeing it in IMAX made the ride even more immersive, every shadow and whisper blown up larger than life.

This one was a mindfuck. You have to follow closely, watch for connections, and maybe even rewatch to piece it all together. It was spooky, trippy, and entertaining in that way that lingers. The scares hit, the tension builds, and the gross-out moments push you right to the edge. It’s the right balance of uncomfortable and compelling — one of those rare scary movies that’s just as fun to revisit as it is to survive the first time.

title: A Complete Unknown
review:
This one sits firmly in the prestige biopic lane — the kind of movie that lives or dies depending on how much you care about the subject. Timothée Chalamet gives it his all, embodying Bob Dylan with eccentric charm, and the film captures that era’s vibe with authenticity. For fans, it’s an absolute treat; for the uninitiated, it’s more of a slow, reverent watch.

From our perspective, it was… fine. Interesting to see Dylan’s quirks and how much of a weirdo he really was, but it didn’t change how we felt about him going in. Great acting, sure, but the story itself never hit us with anything astonishing or memorable. If you’re already a Dylan person, this one’s for you. If not, it might just feel like homework.

title: Companion
review:

If you’re into tech, thrillers, or just want a cheeky mystery with futuristic vibes, this one hits.

title: Paddington in Peru
review:
Paddington is one of those rare movie characters who feels timeless — the kind of figure who can charm kids, parents, and even cynical adults all at once. Paddington in Peru continues that tradition, proving that a family film doesn’t need to be dumbed down or trapped in “kid issues.” Instead, it delivers a heartfelt story with real-life themes, told through the gentle eyes of a small, polite bear who carries big wisdom.

This was a feel-good movie through and through. Cute, wholesome, and entertaining whether you’re watching alone, with friends, or with family. It’s one of those films that leaves you smiling without even realizing it.

Beyond the sweetness, it’s a well-crafted story that balances humor, sincerity, and cultural depth. A kid’s movie on the surface, but one with genuine life lessons tucked inside. That’s the magic of Paddington — simple on the outside, surprisingly profound underneath.

title: Heart Eyes
review:

Heart Eyes slides into the opposite lane — a campy, playful horror-comedy that mixes romance with blood splatter. It matters because it proves there’s still room for cheeky fun in the genre, reminding audiences that horror can be spooky and sweet all at once. Perfect for date night, or for anyone who loves their scares with a side of cheese.

This one delivers exactly what it promises. The acting works, the story entertains, and the balance of romance, cheesiness, and carnage keeps it light without losing its slasher edge. It’s not groundbreaking, but it doesn’t need to be — just a fun, rewatchable ride with enough twists to stay interesting.

title: Las Tres Sisters
review:
Family drama mixed with comedy has always had deep resonance, but it’s rare to see it done with both grit and humor through a Latin American / Mexican American lens with authenticity. Las Tres Sisters matters because it reflects a side of culture—voices, settings, sibling mess, and awkward reconnections—that doesn’t always get Hollywood’s spotlight. It leans into the idea that healing in families isn’t tidy, and sometimes the funniest moments come in the midst of the pain.

This one hits a lot of the emotion. Watching sisters torn apart by time and old wounds being forced back into each other’s orbits is messy, real, and strangely uplifting. The performances are strong—each sister has weight; the comedic moments land without undercutting the drama. Some scenes drag, and a few emotional beats feel a bit expected, but the beauty of the Mexico landscapes, the cultural specificity, and the familial humor keep it grounded and relatable.

What makes it worth watching is how it resonates. If you grew up around sisters, or know what it’s like to carry guilt or resentment in a family, this one will hit you in the chest. And even if you don’t, the heart of it is big enough that you still feel something—laughs, tears, or that tight sympathy for flawed people trying to reconnect.

review:

The only reason this wasn’t a straight-up one-star is because of the sister-brother bond. That relationship carried the whole thing and gave it just enough emotion to keep me watching. Outside of that? Dumb as fuck. The storyline, the acting, the action — all of it felt sloppy.

Same deal from the brain side. If you’re into generic action flicks, maybe this scratches an itch. But nothing about it stands out besides the female lead’s devotion to her brother. Everything else is predictable, cliché, and forgettable.

title: The Monkey
review:
Stephen King adaptations always spark curiosity because you know you’re getting something dark, weird, and just a little unsettling. The Monkey fits neatly in that lane — a horror story with a supernatural object at its core, pulling characters into a spiral of dread. It echoes the Final Destination formula, turning fate itself into the villain, but with that King-style psychological edge layered on top.

It was hard to watch at times, especially the strained, cringey dynamic between the brothers. That made the emotional core difficult to consume, but the movie as a whole was still well-done. Creepy, artsy, and a solid horror flick with a nasty little hook.

It worked as a mind-twister. Not always the most visually pleasant, but that discomfort added to the vibe. And hey, what else can you expect from King? A weird, unnerving idea stretched into a movie that feels true to his brand — flawed, sure, but compelling enough to stick.

title: Last Breath
review:
Survival dramas always find their place because they strip humanity down to its rawest instincts: endurance, sacrifice, and the relentless drive to live. The Last Breath taps into that timeless lane, giving us a story where the odds are stacked against everyone but the spirit to keep fighting refuses to die. It’s part of the larger conversation about resilience — how far we can go, and what it means to hold on for ourselves and for the people around us.

This movie hit as both inspirational and heartbreaking. It was hard to watch at times, but seeing that determination — the drive to survive, to save others, to push through when it seemed impossible — made it powerful. The kind of story that leaves you thinking about your own limits long after the credits roll.

While undeniably inspirational, it sometimes stretches believability. The choices and outcomes feel heightened for effect, making it less realistic and more like a cinematic version of survival. Still, it’s well put together and engaging, with strong performances that keep you locked in.

title: Mickey 17
review:
Every few years, a big-budget sci-fi comes along that tries to shake up the genre with big ideas and even bigger visuals. Mickey 17 is one of those swings — directed by Bong Joon Ho, fronted by Robert Pattinson, and packed with futuristic, dystopian energy. It matters because it’s part of the trend of studios betting on cerebral, high-concept sci-fi while still trying to deliver blockbuster entertainment. ￼

Honestly, I don’t even remember what the message of this movie was supposed to be. But I do remember it was entertaining. Clever, outside the box, and definitely expensive — the kind of film that’s more about the ride than the resolution. The acting worked, the villain was hateable in all the right ways, and the characters leaned into the chaos in a way that kept it fun to watch, even if it was messy.

Pattinson can carry just about anything, and this was no different. The world-building had weight, the sci-fi concepts had bite, and even though it’s not the kind of movie I’d normally be into, it carved out its space. It’s science-y, dystopian, and maybe a little too wild for its own good — but there’s an audience for that, and this movie found it.

title: Magazine Dreams
review:
Magazine Dreams lands hard because it pulls back the curtain on obsessed ambition — the kind that wears you down even as you chase the spotlight. It matters because this isn’t just another success story: it’s about how far someone is willing to push themselves, body and mind, for a dream that might never return the love you pour into it. The film digs into body image, mental health, and the cost of being seen.

This one left me with a weird, heavy feeling. It was heartbreaking to watch — you root for him so much, but also hope he stops and can find help. The world of competitive bodybuilding is one we rarely get on screen, especially with this much internal chaos. After the credits, it stuck with me. But enjoyment? Not really. It was uncomfortable, more pain than uplift.

The film tried. Jonathan Majors gives a committed performance as Killian Maddox, and there are moments where vulnerability cuts through the discomfort. But the craft felt uneven — the storyline often sliding into pain without payoff, scenes that dragged, and emotional beats that teetered between raw and repetitive. It’s not a film you walk out feeling good, but it’s one you walk out feeling moved.

title: Black Bag
review:
Black Bag hits because espionage isn’t just about codes and betrayals — it’s about the humans caught in between. Directed by Steven Soderbergh and starring Cate Blanchett and Michael Fassbender, it wraps moral gray areas, action, and suspicion into a marriage story you can’t help but feel. It matters because it asks: who do you trust when you can’t trust your own heart?

This movie was insane. At its core, it feels like a love story built on trust, constantly asking whether you should believe your partner or doubt them. Some twists were predictable, others blindsided me, but the way it unfolded was gripping. The action scenes were sharp, the mystery kept me guessing, and the emotional stakes made it more than just another spy flick. For me, it was a blast — one of the better espionage thrillers I’ve seen in a while.

It wasn’t my typical go-to, but I can respect how it worked. There were moments where it felt heavy, where the tension between loyalty to love and loyalty to country cut deep. Blanchett and Fassbender carry so much weight (their chemistry pulls you in), but it’s the smaller characters too — the betrayals, the secrets, the paranoia — that lift the story. Some stuff felt a little familiar, but Black Bag earns its payoff more than it drowns in its clichés.

title: Novocaine
review:
In a sea of superhero fatigue, Novacaine carves out its own lane: part action flick, part love story, part ridiculous what-if premise. It matters because it plays with a universal fantasy — what would life look like if you literally couldn’t feel pain? It’s absurd, sure, but also strangely relatable. The film leans all the way in, mixing wild stunts, messy romance, and tongue-in-cheek storytelling into a chaotic package.

It’s refreshing, fun, and ridiculous in all the right ways. The lead shrugs off things no human could realistically survive, but that’s the point — this is a movie that knows it’s unbelievable and has fun with it. The twists, the romance, and the chaos all work together to keep it entertaining. Not your typical superhero story, more like a grounded “what if” shot through with adrenaline. The no-pain gimmick sparks some clever set pieces, and the lead sells it enough to make you wonder where his career heads next.

title: Locked
review:
High-concept thrillers that trap the action inside a single space (Phone Booth, Buried) live or die on acting and tension. Locked joins that lane, proving you don’t need explosions or sprawling sets to grip an audience. Instead, it builds suspense through dialogue, desperation, and the weight of consequences. It matters because it shows how the right performances — paired with a sharp hook — can keep you glued to the screen without ever leaving the driver’s seat.

This one hooks you fast. Watching a struggling father dig himself deeper with each bad choice is both heartbreaking and riveting. The claustrophobic car setting forces every ounce of drama to come from the performances, and it works. Anthony Hopkins as the ominous car owner elevates the film, adding menace and gravitas that stick with you. It’s the kind of thriller that begs for a second watch once it hits streaming.

On the craft side, this is a tight execution of a risky concept. Not your average action flick — more like a morality play on wheels. The premise is simple but effective: pay the piper or face the cost. Proof that all you really need is a sharp idea and actors who can sell it.

title: The Amateur
review:
The Amateur pushes into the tragic love-story lane wrapped in espionage — less about saving the world, more about a man who’s lost everything and is willing to burn it all down. Directed by James Hawes and starring Rami Malek, Rachel Brosnahan, Laurence Fishburne, and more, it sits in that category of ordinary people turned unstoppable by grief. It matters because grief is a powerful fuel, and this movie uses the spy-ops framework to ask: what do you do when your love is your last reason to keep going. ￼

I really enjoyed this one. Watching Charlie, clearly out of his depth, fight tooth and nail because he had nothing left to lose was gripping. The acting sold it — you felt for him, even as he tore everyone down. It scratched the same itch as that movie where Gerard Butler run circles around the justice system from a jail cell.

It’s a fine movie. Good acting, solid tension, well put together. It’s just not the kind of spy thriller I naturally gravitate toward — the emotional moments hit harder for some than others, and at times it leaned into tropes. Still, for what it tries to do, it mostly works.

title: Working Man

title: The Legend of Ochi
review:
In an era where family films often default to loud spectacle, The Legend of Ochi takes a slower, more artistic route. It matters because it continues that trend of animated or fantasy-leaning stories that weave digestible life lessons for kids while nudging at heavier themes for adults. At its core, it’s about pushing back against fear, trusting your intuition, and seeing past what people tell you to believe.

The film tells the story of a young girl who befriends a misunderstood creature, flipping the script on what her community says about him. It’s touching, even inspirational, as it leans into the idea of breaking from the herd and trusting your morals. That said, the pacing drags at times, and while the creature design is cute and charming, the story itself doesn’t quite reach the heights it’s aiming for. Watching it with kids makes sense — they’ll find Ochi adorable, and adults will catch the deeper metaphors — but on its own, it can feel a little dull.

title: Sinners
review:
Every so often, a film drops that feels like it shouldn’t exist anymore — a gritty, relentless thriller that keeps you strapped in for hours without ever letting up. Sinners is that kind of movie. With shades of From Dusk Till Dawn but its own original flair, it digs into themes of family, loyalty, toxic faith, and survival, all wrapped in a pulpy, action-packed story. It matters because films this raw and unpolished rarely make it to theaters now, and when they do, they stand out like a shot of adrenaline in a year of over-processed blockbusters.

From the opening moments, the story hooks you with its start-at-the-ending framing device, pulling you into the question of how we got here. Across just a couple of days, chaos unravels, and every revelation hits harder than the last. The family dynamics — strained father-son tensions, uncles who will stop at nothing for blood ties — add weight to the violence, making the story about more than just shootouts and carnage. At its core, it’s about the brotherhood we choose and the bonds we inherit, the trust and loyalty that drive people to go to war for their community, even against impossible odds. Beneath the violence and imbalance of the world, there’s also a quieter thread — a raw desire to live, to hold on, and to keep loving the people who matter most.

It’s long, it’s packed, and it’s captivating throughout. The mix of suspense, action, and even bits of romance makes it feel full without ever tipping into excess. By the time the ending hits, it lands with both tragedy and revelation — the kind of twist that sticks with you. Maybe it won’t hit everyone the same way, but for those who love unflinching thrillers, this one feels like a rare gem.

title: Final Destination Bloodlines
review:
Somehow, after two decades of elaborate death traps and Rube Goldberg-style chaos, Final Destination still has juice left in the tank. Bloodlines leans into everything fans come for: tension, fake-outs, and the sick thrill of watching the inevitable unfold.

What makes this one stand out is how it folds family history and flashbacks into the formula, tying the deaths to a deeper lineage without losing the popcorn fun. It’s cheesy, sure, but that’s part of the ride — it knows exactly what kind of movie it is.

The suspense works because the movie plays with your nerves like a fiddle. Every setup makes you clench, waiting for the worst possible outcome, and just when you think you’ve guessed it, the film swerves.

That anticipation — that slow, painful pump-fake — is what keeps the theater buzzing. Add in a cast that’s fun enough to root for (and laugh at), and you’ve got one of the strongest entries in the franchise. It’s not reinventing the wheel, but it doesn’t need to. The wheel is spinning, the blood is flowing, and death still wins.

title: Fight or Flight
review:
Airplane thrillers have their own subgenre DNA — tight quarters, limited escape, and the pressure cooker of strangers trapped together. Fight or Flight leans into that formula but dresses it up with Josh Hartnett (yep, he’s back) and a mix of martial arts spectacle with Hollywood polish. It matters because it scratches the itch for pure action escapism at a time when audiences are still chasing high-concept blockbusters that don’t ask too much from the brain.

The movie is pretty much what you’d expect: nonstop brawls, creative set pieces, and a few outlandish “what the fuck” moments that feel pulled out of a kung fu wire-fu playbook. It’s entertaining in that airplane-movie way — not groundbreaking, but fun enough to kill a couple hours. Hartnett brings enough charm to make it watchable, and while the plot isn’t reinventing anything, it finds small ways to keep things fresh. By setting everything inside the plane, the filmmakers leaned hard on the acting and close-quarters choreography, which actually works in the movie’s favor.

Not great, not terrible — just solid, popcorn-friendly action that’s best enjoyed with your tray table locked and seat back upright.

title: Lilo & Stitch
review:
Live-action remakes are always tricky — too faithful, and you risk being stale; too different, and you alienate the diehards. Disney keeps mining its animated vault, and Stitch was always going to be a tough one. The cultural footprint is massive, the Elvis needle-drops iconic, and the Ohana message timeless. So when this dropped, it mattered because it wasn’t just another remake — it was Disney trying to bottle lightning twice, during a strike year no less.

And that strike context shows. The movie feels oddly stiff, like the actors weren’t allowed to breathe or improv, leaving performances that don’t always land. Some casting choices felt off, and key beats were either missing or rushed. Elvis barely gets his due, which is wild considering how much he anchored the original vibe. But even with those gaps, there are still moments that work — the ocean, the chaos, the heartstrings of family sticking together. You feel flashes of what made the cartoon a classic.

Nostalgia really does a lot of the heavy lifting here. It’s fun to see certain scenes come to life in live-action, and Stitch remains a cultural juggernaut who still hits kids and adults alike. The film is uneven, yes, but it manages to thread enough of the original spirit while setting up room for sequels. If nothing else, it’s proof that Stitch is here to stay.

title: Bring Her Back
review:
The hype was real for this one. Coming from the directors of Talk to Me, expectations were sky-high, especially after how strong their debut landed in the horror space. They’ve been branded as the new faces of elevated, grotesque horror — so naturally, Bring Her Back was supposed to be their victory lap. Instead, it sparked one of those “love it or hate it” conversations. Was it pushing boundaries, or just pushing buttons?

For me, it leaned into the latter. The concept, zoomed out, is strong: grief, morality, the impossible choices wrapped in horror fantasy. On paper, it should hit. But the execution was messy — gross, gory, sometimes just plain nasty in ways that weren’t scary so much as off-putting. The story was hard to follow, the weirdness sometimes overwhelmed the weight of the emotions, and instead of leaving the theater shaken in the best way, I left just… annoyed. Maybe it was my own high expectations, maybe it’s a rewatch that changes everything, but my gut reaction was straight-up hate.

Still, I can admit it’s not all trash. There’s an unpredictability here that works. You don’t know where the story’s headed, the characters are bizarrely compelling, and the directors clearly have a knack for twisting the familiar into the grotesque. The problem is the balance — for every smart idea, there’s a moment that feels indulgent or just there to gross you out. I can respect the swing, but it wasn’t the kind of horror I wanted.

title: The Life of Chuck
review:
Based on Stephen King’s novella, The Life of Chuck isn’t your standard inspirational drama — it’s a cosmic riff on memory, mortality, and what it means to exist at all. Told in reverse, the film breaks into three sections, pulling us from the end of a man’s life back to his childhood. That structure alone sets it apart, letting the story feel both intimate and universal, a meditation on how a single human can hold entire worlds inside them. In a movie landscape that often leans predictable, this one dares to be strange, emotional, and profoundly trippy.

Watching it unfold backwards feels disorienting at first, but then the rhythm clicks. Characters splinter into different storylines, only to fold back together later in ways that expand the whole picture. By the time you realize what the film is really doing, it’s already gotten under your skin.

The acting — from the younger cast to the veteran leads — grounds the metaphysical weirdness, giving it warmth and gravity. It’s not an easy watch for everyone. If you’re more about clean storytelling and simple arcs, this might feel like emotional indulgence. But if you’re open to the ride, it’s captivating and heartfelt in a way that sticks with you long after.

title: Friendship
review:
At a glance, Friendship looks like another offbeat buddy comedy in the vein of I Love You, Man. But instead of playing it safe, it dives into the awkward, often cringeworthy truth of what it means to connect with another person as an adult. Casting Paul Rudd in a role that flips his usual charm on its head is a clever move — he’s not the easygoing everyman this time, but a character that forces you to ask: is this guy even likable?

That alone makes it stand out in today’s comedy landscape, where formula usually wins over discomfort. And discomfort is exactly what makes this movie work. Some scenes are hilarious in their strangeness, while others feel almost too real, pulling up old wounds of broken connections, failed friendships, or times when you’ve been that awkward person in the room. Depending on where you’re coming from, it either makes you laugh or squirm — maybe both. That duality is what gives Friendship its edge. It’s not an easy watch, but it’s a bold one.

title: I Don’t Understand You
review:
At its core, I Don’t Understand You thrives on the universal frustration of miscommunication. It’s the kind of story where one wrong move spirals into a chain of misunderstandings, and by the time you think it might settle, the stakes reset and the chaos starts again. These films are hard to pull off without feeling repetitive, but here the writing is quick, witty, and full of clever detours that keep it fresh. The humor comes less from punchlines and more from watching people get tangled in their own bad decisions — a theme that feels both painfully relatable and wildly entertaining.

The pacing is brisk, and the movie constantly finds new ways to twist the knife, surprising you at every turn. It’s a fast ride, but not an empty one — the layers of irony and the occasional moral dilemma make it smarter than your average comedy of errors. At times it feels like an off-the-beaten-path indie flick, the kind you’re glad you stumbled into, and by the end you’re left grinning at just how absurdly everything unraveled. Not perfect, but sharp, fun, and absolutely worth the rewatch we waited for.

title: Dangerous Animals
review:
There’s something uniquely unsettling about thrillers that feel like they could happen. Dangerous Animals taps straight into that primal fear — traveling somewhere unfamiliar, meeting the wrong kind of people, and realizing too late you’re trapped in their game. It’s part survival thriller, part cautionary tale, all set against the eerie isolation of the open water. The film leans heavy on tension and brutality, but it never strays too far into the unbelievable. That realism is what makes it stick.

At its core, this is a story about willpower — about one woman’s refusal to quit even as everything stacks against her. The film thrives on that raw hunter-versus-prey dynamic, and it’s surprisingly captivating for a premise that could’ve easily slipped into cliché. There’s violence, theatrics, and a few “what the fuck” moments, but it also carries an undercurrent of truth: sometimes survival isn’t just about fighting off predators, it’s about seeing the predator inside ordinary people. That’s the part that lingers when the credits roll.

It’s meant to be the torch-passing film, the “Legends” chapter that ties everything together.

And while that all sounds great, the truth is the movie never really kicks above “fine.” Nostalgia keeps it watchable, but the story itself is basic — training montages, rivalries, redemption arcs, rinse and repeat. It has moments that hit (some sweet, some crowd-pleasing), but they’re surrounded by predictability. If you grew up with the franchise, you’ll probably smile a few times. If you didn’t, this won’t be the movie to make you a fan. At the end of the day, it’s more wax than shine.

title: Materialists
review:
Romantic comedies have been missing from the mainstream rotation, and Materialist makes a case for why they still belong. Dakota Johnson has basically taken the genre on her shoulders, keeping the tradition alive with a mix of charm, wit, and modern absurdity. It leans into that glossy “slice of rich people life,” full of yachts, penthouses, and drama that’s entertaining precisely because of how ridiculous it feels. In a world where everyone is chasing “what matters,” the movie cheekily asks: do you even know what that is?

It plays like Hitch with a gender flip, wrapped in a toxic love triangle that somehow still manages to be funny and weirdly sweet. The characters make questionable decisions, but the cast sells it — Dakota Johnson in particular feels magnetic, balancing surface-level confidence with moments of real vulnerability. The twists are trippy and “WTF” enough to keep you watching, even when the story itself doesn’t dig too deep. You’ll laugh, you’ll cringe, and you might roll your eyes, but you’ll also walk away oddly satisfied.

title: 40 Acres
review:
40 Acres drops us into a tense, survivalist drama built around family, resilience, and the hard choices that ripple through a community. It’s part love letter to mothers who hold everything together, part cautionary tale about how even small mistakes can cost everything in worlds this unforgiving. The film thrives on its cat-and-mouse sequences, those “how the hell are they getting out of this?” moments that pull you in even when the tone stays grim.

The family dynamic is the beating heart — watching a mom balance tenderness and ferocity while her kids try to navigate a brutal reality keeps the story grounded. Some scenes hit with raw emotion, while others feel more like a creative showcase for tension and spectacle. Visually it’s strong, and narratively it keeps you on edge, though it doesn’t always reach the heights it aims for. Still, the blend of survival instincts, loyalty, and sacrifice makes it more memorable than the average thriller.

title: 28 Years Later
review:
This is a revival nobody saw coming. After 28 Days Later and 28 Weeks Later aged into cringe territory, expectations were low — but 28 Years Later came out swinging. It feels like a redemption of the franchise: sharper direction, layered storytelling, and a willingness to actually wrestle with big themes like survival, family, and the morality of hope. The title itself speaks volumes — nearly three decades of endurance, grief, and adaptation condensed into a brutal survival tale that asks: what kind of people are left when the world never recovers?

What stood out most wasn’t just the infected chaos, but the human core. The bond between the father and son was unsettling — a dad projecting strength while hiding weakness, teaching bravery through lies, and leaving his kid to pick up the moral weight. The son’s decision to take his mother to the doctor — and the sheer trail of death it triggered — gave the film a prophetic energy, like destiny moving through a child. Every death stung harder because these weren’t day-one survivors; these were people who had lasted decades, only to fall over a slip, a mistake, or someone else’s choice.

There’s a haunting ambiguity too — the doctor who quietly survived alone for years, clinging to purpose without despair. The phone and internet references that blur whether this world is rebuilding or just clinging to scraps. The ending, with the white-masked mercenaries, sets up more stories — because if we’re moving past “trilogy,” we’re now in saga territory.

Creepy, freaky, and at times frustrating, but undeniably gripping. A film that proves survival horror isn’t about the monsters at all — it’s about the fragile, flawed people who live long enough to still matter.

title: Jurassic World Rebirth
review:
After the messy sprawl of the last few Jurassic World films, Rebirth felt like a reset. Instead of bloated spectacle, Universal leaned into straight-up horror-action: people trapped, dinosaurs hunting, greed fueling the chaos. It strips the franchise down to what always worked — humans playing god, then paying the price. This time, Scarlett Johansson steps into the mix, and she brings enough grit and gravity to keep the movie from feeling like just another cash-grab sequel.

It’s not revolutionary, but it’s refreshingly simple. The kills hit, the tension builds, and the set pieces remind you how terrifying dinosaurs can be when filmmakers actually let them be predators instead of background CGI. The human story is still built on the same beats — greed, arrogance, and misplaced family values — but that’s also the point: the cycle never ends, only mutates.

On one hand, it’s just another Jurassic World entry, polished but familiar. On the other, it’s proof that when this series embraces its horror roots, it still has teeth.

title: F1
review:
Racing movies are tricky — they either lean too heavy on the gearhead jargon or go so broad that fans roll their eyes. F1 threads the line perfectly. It marries the spectacle of Formula 1 with a story that works even if you don’t care about the sport. Think Moneyball with more horsepower: a film that teaches you the intricacies of its world without ever losing the entertainment value of the drama.

Brad Pitt proves, once again, that he can do no wrong. He brings grit, wisdom, and that veteran calm opposite a fiery young lead who absolutely delivers. Toss in a sharp, shady performance from the Latin antagonist (Emilio — unforgettable energy) and you’ve got a film brimming with tension, heart, and clever twists. The visuals are insane — IMAX puts you right on the track, every engine growl rattling your ribcage.

It’s not just about racing; it’s about mentorship, risk, ego, and survival in a machine that never stops moving. From the toxic politics behind the scenes to the pure thrill of the race itself, F1 nails the balance. It’s a sports flick for the die-hards and the casuals alike — a high-octane drama that left us buzzing.

title: The Phoenician Scheme
review:
This one lives in that elevated indie-thriller lane — the kind of film meant to spark conversation more than deliver thrills in the traditional sense. But in theaters? It lands differently. The tension is sharper, the visuals more hypnotic, the cast pulling you into their eccentric orbit. Even when the plot leaves you scratching your head — “What even is the Phoenician scheme?” — it keeps you hooked. The ending twist is unpredictable, the ensemble carries every odd beat, and you can’t deny the craft.

title: Superman
review:
Superhero fatigue is real — walking into this one, expectations weren’t high. But Superman actually worked. The story leaned less on endless DCU-style connections and more on making Superman feel both human and larger-than-life at the same time. It had moments that made you think, moments that hit surprisingly hard, and set pieces that finally captured what it should mean to have someone invincible fighting for us.

The film wasn’t perfect — some cheesier beats, like Superdog, didn’t land if you’re not nostalgic for the comics. For people who never vibed with Superman as a character, there’s still that barrier of “he’s only weak to a rock from space.” But the way the action was staged — waves of enemies against one man who couldn’t be stopped — gave it a comic-book energy that finally felt earned instead of cheap.

It’s a Superman film that stands tall on its own. Even for skeptics, it’s hard not to admit: this one was good.

title: Together
review:
This one had us walking in with high expectations — Dave Franco and Alison Brie already set the bar — and it didn’t disappoint. The film balances a strange mix of romance and psychological thriller, unfolding at a pace that’s sometimes slow but always simmering with unease. There are moments that make you laugh at the absurdity, and moments that make you squirm with discomfort. It’s a film that asks what it means to merge your life with someone else — how much of yourself you give, what you risk, and what you gain — all while dangling the audience in suspense.

It’s unique, it’s unsettling, and it’s memorable. A romance, a thriller, and a mirror for anyone questioning what “forever” really means.

title: Oh, Hi!
review:
Comedy built on chaos is nothing new, but Oh Hi finds that sweet spot where humor meets relatability. It’s not slapstick or over-polished — it’s the kind of comedy that feels ripped from the randomness of real life. In a time when people crave both laughter and authenticity, this film captures how one or two small choices can snowball into a storm, while still grounding itself in loyalty, friendship, and the ride-or-die bonds that hold people together.

Oh Hi hit home for me. It leaned into those perfectly timed dominoes of life, where absurdity feels both magical and real. The couples felt familiar — I saw myself in the main relationship and even in the friends who crash in. The loyalty, the ride-or-die energy, the refusal to let each other fail — that stuck. Sure, the movie strayed into surreal moments, but it always landed with that “this could happen to anyone” vibe. By the end, it was beautifully ambiguous who was sane, who was crazy, or if anyone was — and that uncertainty made it even more lovely.

On craft, this is sharp. Watching one or two bad decisions unravel into something bigger keeps you leaning in. The surprises are paced well, the payoff lands, and I’d watch it again. It’s the kind of movie that works on date night — funny, thoughtful, and endlessly rewatchable.

title: She Rides Shotgun
review:
She Rides Shotgun is more than a crime thriller — it’s a meditation on loyalty, survival, and the bond between parent and child when the world’s already stacked against them. It sits in that lane of poetic, gritty storytelling that feels both hyperreal and mythic, where criminals and cops blur into shades of human struggle. It asks: do your circumstances define you, or do your choices?

From the jump, the movie builds tension around whether the dad is truly guilty of the crimes pinned on him, or just caught in a web of bad circumstances. Watching him pick up his daughter sets the tone: she’s not naïve, she’s sharp. Intuitive. Calling out lies adults tell kids to “protect” them. By the middle of the film, her intelligence and awareness aren’t just quirks — they’re survival skills.

The standout moments hit hard. The scene where she fires the gun, and the dad sees her humanity break under the weight of that act — heartbreaking. You could feel his guilt as much as his love. And later, his sacrifice, walking away into the light like he already knew his fate, while his daughter ran after him — pure cinematic poetry. The firefight at the end maybe went a little overboard, but the emotional core stayed intact: bravery, resilience, and the cost of survival.

What really sticks is how the film balanced grit with hope. The daughter’s strength at the end — scarred but steady, pushing forward “one foot in front of the other” like her dad taught her — left me shaken. She’s a boss, and you know she’ll carry that lesson for life. The final shot, with her finding a kind home and peers to bond with, carried both sorrow and peace. That duality is what made the film so affecting.

title: Freakier Friday
review:
The 2025 sequel taps directly into the energy of the original Freaky Friday, but with a modern sensibility. It’s part of this recent wave of reboots that finally seem to “get it” — honoring what made the originals iconic while resisting the urge to spoil the best bits in the trailers. Instead, Freakier Friday keeps plenty of its humor and heartfelt twists hidden, rewarding audiences who show up without overexposure. It’s a family comedy that knows its audience spans generations, balancing nostalgia with fresh energy.

The biggest win here is how natural it felt. The callbacks, references, and returning characters were handled in ways that felt fun instead of forced. It’s almost like the filmmakers finally built the movie the way our brains always thought sequels should be built growing up — keep the world intact, bring back familiar faces, drop in clever little surprises, and don’t ruin it all in the promo cycle.

Nostalgia hits strong, but it’s not just fan service — the story itself has a real impact, carrying a heartfelt family message that lands across audiences. Whether you grew up with the first one or you’re just catching this new version, it works as both a standalone and a continuation.

In the end, it felt like a true “shift in time.” A sequel that doesn’t just recycle, but reflects the way people actually want movies to evolve.

title: Weapons
review:
Weapons cements itself as one of those ambitious, interwoven narrative thrillers that dares to cross perspectives, blur morality, and challenge the audience to sit in discomfort. It’s not a franchise grab or a popcorn throwaway — it’s part of the wave of modern horror/thriller hybrids that push psychological unease and social commentary into the mainstream. With its layered structure, shifting POVs, and morally tangled core, it forces you to confront how messy humanity can get when survival, guilt, and fear clash.

From the opening shot — a faceless figure you somehow already recognize — the film grips you. The narration by a child outside the central events makes it even more haunting, setting a tone of innocence watching horror unfold. The story plays like a series of dominoes: one perspective ends in shock, the next picks up just a little further down the line, overlapping and reframing everything you thought you knew. That momentum keeps pushing until you’re knee-deep in chaos, watching a town turn against a girl while every side feels simultaneously justified and unforgivable.

It’s suffocating at times — fight after fight, twist after twist — but that relentlessness is intentional. The film is designed to exhaust you, to leave you in that “nobody really wins” headspace. And while it’s not the kind of ending you walk out of feeling good about, the craftsmanship is undeniable. The main actress carries it hard, her presence anchoring a story that could have easily collapsed under its own weight. Even when the pieces felt unexplainable, the sheer tension and artistry made it worth sticking through.

It’s not perfect, it’s not comforting, and it’s not an easy rewatch. But it’s unforgettable — a horror-thriller that digs under your skin and stays there.

title: Relay
review:
Relay slides into that niche of action-thrillers that are both slick and strangely grounded. It’s not just bullets and car chases — it leans into process, systems, and the way corruption trickles down to ordinary people who get caught in the crossfire. With its emphasis on middle-men, handoffs, and layers of secrecy, the film mirrors real-world business and political shadows, where accountability gets buried under endless intermediaries. It also deserves credit for weaving accessibility into its DNA, highlighting how communication tools (like relay interpreting for the deaf community) shift dynamics in tense, high-stakes situations.

Relay hooked us more than expected. The stylish cinematography, sharp sound design, and clever pacing gave it that “Bourne Identity but fresh” type of vibe. The whole conceit of middle-men calling on other middle-men was fascinating — a rabbit hole of power dynamics and misdirection where every time you thought the net had closed, it slipped wider open. The characters carried the weight, especially in those moments when naivety clashed with survival instincts. Yes, some choices felt unbelievably dumb, but that’s also what kept the tension high: watching someone stumble into disaster while you’re screaming, “don’t do it!”

There were definitely points where it got confusing, maybe because we missed the first few minutes, maybe because the film wanted us disoriented. Either way, it landed. The relay concept itself was eye-opening — whether factually airtight or not, it added texture to the story, and seeing it all come together was worth the ride. It’s not perfect, but it’s the kind of thriller that leaves you chewing over its structure, its “what ifs,” and its commentary on how messy the truth can get when nobody’s hands are clean.

title: The Knife
review:
The Knife pushes into that rare space where a thriller doubles as a mirror. It’s less about what happened and more about how people tell what they think happened — how memory gaps, fear, race, and survival instincts twist the narratives that stick harder than facts. In an era when headlines often outpace reality, this film feels chillingly relevant. It captures how stories are spun — by police reports, by neighbors, by families protecting their own — and how those spins shape public belief, regardless of what’s true.

This one shook me. The ending left me questioning everything — not because the film was unclear, but because it was built to push you into that fog of perspective. Did we defend a man who was secretly guilty, or did small human mistakes spiral into a tragedy the system repackaged in its own image? The final radio call reframed the dad as a criminal — even though we never saw proof. It reminded me how easily decisions, skin color, and circumstance can be weaponized into a narrative that sticks, especially when the lens favors some stories over others.

Watching it, I reflected on memory itself — how we miss, how we omit, how we defend. Brianna pointed out details I’d ignored, and we pieced things together differently. No one sees the same story. Nobody is entirely right, nobody entirely wrong, and everyone is trying to protect a version of themselves. The Knife turned that mess into an unsettling, brutal piece of art.

Stripped of overanalysis, it’s simply a well-made, unnerving film. Realistic, tight, and much more thought-provoking than I expected. It kept me engaged from start to finish.

title: Caught Stealing
review:
Caught Stealing is a masterpiece — a film that drags you through every emotion: discomfort, nervous tension, heartbreak, and even fleeting moments of joy. It’s visually stunning. The kinetic way it’s shot — all that running, moving, breathing with the main character — puts you inside his fractured, fragile world. From the very beginning, you sense what’s wrong, but the movie lets it unravel slowly, confirming suspicions piece by piece while letting trauma seep into every decision.

The lead character is both kind and broken, damaged yet compelling, his trauma surfacing in ways that shape the entire story. Following him feels like chasing someone constantly in motion, brushing against strangers and friends alike, each encounter exposing another piece of who he is. The supporting cast sharpens this even further, testing him, pressuring him, reflecting his wounds back at him.

What makes Caught Stealing stand apart is the ending. Movies so often hand us a neat resolution, a glossy bow. This one doesn’t. It gives us survival, but scarred survival — a bittersweet outcome that feels more honest than any “dream ending.” He made it through, but not into perfection, not into what he wanted. And that realism hit harder than any twist could, because life doesn’t always deliver the dream — sometimes it only leaves you with what’s left.

It hooked me, broke me, and left me in awe. Caught Stealing isn’t about escaping with everything intact. It’s about surviving with whatever pieces remain — and finding a grim kind of mercy in that.

title: The Roses
review:
Relationships are complicated — that’s the thesis here — and Roses doesn’t shy away from the messy, toxic, playful, and heartbreaking parts of being in love with someone for years. At times it feels like a rom-com, at others a tragedy, but the throughline is chemistry. The ending is a gut-punch — a reminder that sometimes waiting to work things out leads to “too late,” and too late is the cruelest outcome of all. It plays like both a love story and a wake-up call: sort it out now, because love is a fire that doesn’t burn forever.

The only offbeat note is the Kate McKinnon/Andy Samberg pairing, which feels a little odd, but doesn’t derail the story. Altogether, it’s a movie that captures love’s contradictions: joyful and toxic, playful and tragic, funny and devastating.

title: Trust
review:
Trust sets itself up as a chilling industry parable — the story of a young celebrity taken advantage of by her senior co-host, manipulated into pregnancy, and then pushed to the edge as he plots to erase her. It’s a premise with weight, one that echoes the real-world whispers and headlines about abuse, coercion, and silencing women in positions of vulnerability. In that sense, it matters: these stories aren’t just fiction, they’re reflections of how power gets weaponized in entertainment and beyond.

But while the concept is potent, the execution doesn’t land as sharply as it should. Performances wobble — the lead actress shows flashes of strength and believability, but the film doesn’t give her enough to elevate the material. At times, it feels like a wasted opportunity: more soap opera than psychological thriller, more cliché than cautionary tale.

There are moments that sting, particularly when the parallels to real industry abuse feel uncomfortably plausible, and Sophie Turner adds depth where she can. Still, the overall result leans more disappointing than devastating — a story that should have left scars but instead fades too quickly.

title: Lurker
review:
At its core, Lurker is an unflinching dive into the toxicity of relationships shaped by ego, insecurity, and proximity to fame. It belongs in the lineage of experimental indie films that don’t just tell a story but force you to feel it — awkward silences, suffocating pauses, and poor decisions stretched until they become unbearable. It’s a movie about how power is often held, not through talent or charisma, but through leverage, secrets, and manipulation. Watching it feels like being trapped in a room with people you’d normally escape from — and that’s exactly the point.

What makes it so effective is also what makes it excruciating. The acting is phenomenal, capturing the tedious awkwardness of group dynamics breaking down in real time. You don’t just see the protagonist make terrible choices — you feel the oxygen leave the room when he does. He’s both decent and poisonous at once, and that contradiction is what makes him so infuriating to watch.

Beneath the surface, the film carries a sharp commentary on mental health. The protagonist believes he’s fine, that his choices are justified, that he’s simply misunderstood — but what we’re really watching is someone unraveling without realizing it. That denial, and the damage it causes to himself and everyone around him, is where Lurker lands its heaviest punch. It’s a reminder that untreated issues don’t just destroy the individual, but ripple through entire communities.

For Blockbuster Wave, this was a split experience: a masterful piece of art on one hand, but one so difficult to endure that it bordered on unbearable. The balance leaves us with admiration and exhaustion in equal measure.

title: The Long Walk
review:
Stephen King’s dystopian vision finally hits the screen, and it’s as disturbing as it is magnetic. At a time when survival games and bleak futures dominate the cultural imagination, The Long Walk carves its own lane — less spectacle, more soul. It’s about endurance, but also about the psychology of companionship, cruelty, and the impossible choices people make under pressure.

The movie works because it’s not just about the walk — it’s about what drives each step. Revenge, grief, hope, pure existence. The two central characters embody opposite poles: one walking for vengeance, the other for life itself. Their chemistry anchors the film, and their final exchange is devastating. It forces you to ask whether free will ever really wins over instinct, or whether darkness has the last word.

This is a film that unsettles you not with jump scares or gore, but with truth. Watching strangers become brothers in days, watching humanity spark in the face of inevitable death — it’s haunting, heartbreaking, and brutally honest about the human condition. The ending leaves you raw, questioning, and maybe even a little broken.

title: The Conjuring: Last Rites
review:

The atmosphere never builds, the tension never sharpens, and instead of feeling haunted, you feel trapped in a theater with a ghost story that won’t end. By the halfway point, the dread comes not from the demons but from realizing this franchise should have bowed out years ago.

That payoff sticks: people don’t always act rationally in crisis, but those cracks are what make them human. It’s not laugh-out-loud perfect, but the mix of humor, grief, and perseverance carries the story through.

title: The Baltimorons
review:
Set against a cozy but complicated Christmas in Baltimore, The Baltimorons walks a thin line between sweet romance and melancholy slice-of-life. It’s very much in the lineage of Harold and Maude or The Graduate — a big age-gap love story that’s bound to be divisive, but handled here with enough warmth and darkly comic touches to keep it compelling. The city itself plays a quiet supporting role, grounding the film in rowhouses, diners, and late-night walks that feel lived-in.

The story follows a man stuck in a toxic relationship who stumbles through a chaotic holiday night, meeting a dentist who turns his day around. What works best is how the film leans into “flow” — one small decision tumbling into the next until he finds himself in a different life by morning. The romance is unconventional, sure, but it’s also about noticing the signs in front of you and choosing not to resist them. It’s messy, strange, and not exactly the cheery energy most people want on Christmas, but that bittersweet edge is part of its charm.

title: In Whose Name?
review:
Kanye West is one of those figures who feels impossible to escape — whether you love him, hate him, or simply feel exhausted by him. Every few years another documentary drops, trying to capture the myth, the madness, the genius, or the implosion. In Whose Name is his latest cinematic mirror, arriving in an era where the lines between performance, breakdown, and cultural commentary blur more than ever. It’s not just about Kanye as a man, but about how we consume him, interpret him, and project onto him.

On the surface, the film doesn’t feel like much more than a recap. We’ve seen many of these clips before — TMZ meltdowns, Instagram rants, messy headlines — so at times it plays like a stitched-together highlight reel. But then, when the camera lingers long enough, there are flashes of something raw. His rants shift from nonsense into brutal truths about control, family, and exploitation. He names the ways he’s boxed in, then doubles down by being uncontainable, making himself the chaos no one else can own.

It’s powerful and frustrating at the same time. You can’t deny the honesty in moments where he’s calling out how his kids are treated, or how he’s reduced to a caricature. At the same time, the editing is rough — almost like the filmmaker both nailed it and botched it, depending on the scene. What emerges is a portrait of Kanye as both martyr and manipulator, Yeezus and man, a figure who wears contradiction as a badge.

It doesn’t change how you feel about him. If you were already out, you’ll stay out. If you still believe there’s a misunderstood prophet buried inside, you’ll find fuel here. But what the doc does succeed at is showing that he’s willing to put his flaws and fury on screen, and that willingness to self-immolate is what makes Kanye endlessly polarizing, endlessly watchable, and endlessly exhausting.

title: Eleanor the Great
review:
This was one of those screenings where the theater itself became part of the film. Everyone locked in, no distractions, no chatter — just collective silence and the sound of tears breaking out at different moments. That respectful stillness magnified the emotional weight.

Eleanor’s journey unfolded slowly at times, but each step forward carried a gravity that built into something unexpectedly cathartic. Yes, you could see where the story was going. An older woman reflecting on life — it’s not reinventing the wheel. But it didn’t need to. What it offered instead was presence: small joys, deep griefs, and those moments when you think you can’t keep going but something compels you to.

And then there was the most unexpected part: inspiration. Watching a 95-year-old not just existing but fully living — spry, witty, reflective, and present — was a revelation. We fear aging, the decline of body and mind, the way life narrows. But Eleanor the Great showed the opposite: that we don’t lose our humanness, our humor, our spark. In fact, Eleanor herself only broke out into film at age 94, continuing into her mid-90s. That truth alone reframes the narrative of aging: it’s never too late to start, to share, to create. Her own words echo it best — you just get up and keep going.

By the end, the payoff was undeniable. It left you raw, reflective, and strangely grateful — the kind of movie that lingers in your chest long after you leave the theater.

title: The Strangers: Chapter 2
review:
Horror franchises thrive on repetition — masked figures, dark woods, blood-soaked survival tales. The Strangers brand leans hard into the “no motive” menace, which can be chilling in theory. But in 2025, when horror has evolved into meta-commentary (Scream VI), prestige dread (Hereditary), and social allegory (Get Out), a story that circles the same chase loop without growth feels more like filler than evolution. Instead of delivering a satisfying ending, it leans on the weight of a future sequel — more franchise setup than a film that stands on its own.

Watching it felt like being stuck in a horror video game on repeat mode. Sure, it managed a couple jump-scare jolts, but mostly it was an exercise in fatigue — characters running, killers never stopping, and no real-world logic holding it together. The lead carried the chaos decently, but even her survival instincts felt less like resilience and more like plot armor. The crowd’s audible groan at the cliffhanger summed it up: instead of catharsis, we left with exhaustion.

title: One Battle After Another
review:
In a year where immigration dominates headlines and activism gets painted in extremes, this film lands like a mirror held up to the chaos. On the surface, it plays like a slick action-thriller — DiCaprio running scared, wide shots of men and cars squaring off, explosions and shootouts. But underneath, it’s about community, rebellion, and the messy truth of good intentions colliding with bad outcomes. These are characters who start by feeding, protecting, and uplifting each other, only to end up blowing up buildings, robbing to fund their cause, and crossing lines they never meant to cross. That tension — good people forced into bad acts — gives the movie a weight that hits differently in today’s cultural climate.

The film even dips into satirical absurdity with something like Operation Christmas (or “Christmas Adventures,” depending on how you hear it). You can’t quite tell if the filmmakers leaned too hard into parody, making these groups look dumb, or if it’s actually close to real history, which would make it chilling. Either way, it lingers. The irony is that the trailer and marketing hardly hinted at this, probably to keep mainstream audiences focused on the action. But once you’re in it, you realize this is very much a movie about borders, power, and rebellion.

And then there are the performances. Leo nails the “decent guy in over his head,” terrified but stubbornly trying to keep his humanity intact while doing what survival demands. The fractured family dynamic adds bite: the wife’s choices cut deep, but the daughter steals the show. She’s straight-up badass — not because anyone pushed her into it, but because her parents lived it and handed her the tools. She chose to pick them up, and that choice gives her arc real power. For a debut (or near-debut), it’s a standout performance.

The real-time rating experience said a lot: bouncing between three and four, never sliding down, but never hitting that five. And maybe the reason it didn’t break through is simple — as much as we respected the characters, we didn’t feel them. Not the mom, not Leo, and barely even the daughter.

title: The Smashing Machine
review:
Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson trading in charisma for vulnerability feels like the movie moment no one saw coming — a grounded, bruising biopic about early mixed martial arts before the UFC era. The Smashing Machine dives into the brutal birth of the sport, where legends were made in dimly lit rings, stitched together between rounds, and addicted to the chaos that defined them. It’s a story of ego, survival, and the loneliness of greatness — the kind of film that challenges the “invincible fighter” myth by showing what’s left when the crowd goes quiet.

There’s something disarming about watching a man built like a tank crumble from the inside out. The film follows Mark Kerr through his rise, his addictions, and the cost of becoming a machine in a sport that feeds on broken men. It’s slow and bruising — not a hype reel, but a heavy meditation on obsession, pain, and the messy balance between love and self-destruction.

The relationship between Kerr and his partner gives the film its volatile pulse. Their love is toxic, raw, and oddly tender — two people clinging to each other while circling the drain. It’s messy, human, and unsettling to watch, but that’s what makes it hit. The small details cut deepest: Kerr’s stoic calm while being stitched up mid-scene, the quiet between fights, the moments where pain becomes normal.

By the close, the story shifts from darkness toward a hard-won calm. It’s less about loss and more about resilience, offering an ending that chooses to honor endurance over despair.

title: Good Boy
review:
In a genre drowning in cheap scares, Good Boy quietly claws out its own lane. It’s horror told from the eye level of a dog — literally. The camera stays low, the perspective disorients, and the result is something unnervingly intimate. The film toys with empathy, flipping the gaze so the viewer becomes the observer of both human fragility and animal confusion. It’s part experimental art film, part emotional endurance test — a strange, unsettling experience that feels closer to a panic dream than a traditional thriller.

There’s something profound buried in all the chaos. The story isn’t just about fear, but about connection — between owner and pet, health and helplessness, and how love sometimes looks like holding on too long. Even when the script stumbles or drags, the craft shines. The lighting, sound, and performance from the “good boy” himself elevate the concept far beyond its premise.

title: Avatar: The Way of Water
review:
James Cameron’s oceanic sequel is the most expensive meditation on nothingness ever filmed. The Way of Water is an engineering marvel — every drop, ripple, and bioluminescent creature rendered to perfection — yet it floats in a strange place between art and simulation. In an era obsessed with spectacle and scale, Cameron’s film asks (perhaps unintentionally) what happens when technology eclipses storytelling. It’s both a triumph of craft and a cautionary tale about cinema’s new god-complex: mastery without mystery.

The first viewing is pure awe. The screen glows, the sound swells, and you sink into it — the immersion works exactly as designed. But on a second pass, the magic fractures. Once the visual shock wears off, you start noticing what’s missing: pulse, tension, soul. It’s stunning, but strangely sterile — a museum of moving images curated by a perfectionist who can’t stop outdoing himself.

Cameron’s control feels absolute yet distant. You start wondering who he’s really making this for — the audience, or his own legacy. The film’s water becomes a metaphor for the whole endeavor: vast, immaculate, and surface-deep. It’s a world you can admire but not inhabit. Even the theater reflects it — the Brain asleep beside me, an old man quietly exiting, you staring at the screen realizing beauty alone isn’t enough to keep you anchored.

title: Roofman
review:
Roofman revisits the myth of the “good-hearted criminal” but grounds it in real emotion and true events. Channing Tatum delivers one of his most quietly compelling roles — a man both gifted and doomed by his own choices. The film sits somewhere between Catch Me If You Can and The Founder, yet resists glamorizing crime. Instead, it paints a portrait of a man caught between cleverness and conscience, survival and self-sabotage. It raises an uncomfortable truth: good people can still make bad decisions, and not everyone gets a chance to outgrow them.

You can’t help but root for him. You feel his desperation, his intelligence, the ache of someone trying to make something of himself — even if he bends rules to do it. By the end, when the real-life interview footage rolls, it lands deeply. You hear voices of those who loved him — the girlfriend, daughters, church members — still speaking with warmth and forgiveness. That’s when the tragedy sharpens: this wasn’t some career criminal, but a man who lost his way, yet never fully lost his humanity.

The film’s pacing drags at times once you know where it’s heading, but its handheld intensity — the shaky chases, the confined moments — keeps things tactile and real. There’s no Hollywood gloss here: just sweat, consequences, and a man stubbornly believing he might still find a clean exit. It’s sad, smart, and oddly hopeful. The kind of story that makes you wonder how many “bad guys” were just one more break away from something different.

title: Unity
review:
UNITY is more than a show; it’s a cultural handshake between Europe and the U.S. Tomorrowland brings its subtle, dreamlike storytelling, while Insomniac layers on its signature high-energy spectacle. Together, they build something that feels both refined and explosive — a rare synthesis in dance music culture. In a climate where live events are constantly pushing to outdo themselves, this collaboration says: immersion is the future.

It matters because it reframes what a “concert” can be. You’re not just watching; you’re inside. It’s a bold experiment in turning the live audience from spectators into travelers — carried through worlds by visuals, score, and design.

From the opening frames, you realize you don’t want to leave your seat. At most concerts, there are natural breaks — time to grab a drink, stretch, take a walk. Not here. The visuals wrap you so completely that stepping out feels like breaking a spell. For two-plus hours, you’re glued, because every second feels like it might reveal another impossible world.

The environments are surreal: alien cities, cosmic oceans, luminous portals. Sometimes it feels like Spy Kids holograms made real, other times like a lucid dream you can’t wake from. The synchronization of music and imagery can overwhelm, but when it hits, it’s euphoric. The live orchestra elevates everything — a human tether beneath the electronic journey.

Yes, the “movie” side of the narrative is messy. Storylines cut, jump, and sometimes dissolve. But the sheer immersion covers the cracks. The crowd energy stitches the gaps, and when the DJ finally takes over, it all fuses — the screen, the sound, the people. You’re not just attending a show, you’re riding it.

Walking out, you’re buzzing. It opens your eyes to what venues like the Sphere can become — gateways to festivals, films, even places we haven’t dreamed of yet. It leaves you with an afterglow: a reminder that entertainment’s future is not just about bigger, but deeper.

title: Tron: Ares
review:
Tron: Ares enters a moment where legacy franchises are trying to figure out how to blend nostalgia with new energy. The movie matters because it leans into the Tron universe’s strongest qualities: worldbuilding, neon visuals, music, and the feeling of stepping into a digital mythology. It exists in that cultural space where the vibe itself is a major part of why people show up, and it joins the ongoing conversation about whether cinematic worlds can carry a film even when the story is imperfect.

The experience was genuinely enjoyable, even with clear flaws. The movie has cheesy moments, noticeable story gaps, and stretches where the visuals and soundtrack clearly received more attention than the actual script. But the entertainment value still lands, especially when you are watching it with someone who reacts, jokes, and stays engaged. The slow start and scattered character intros could feel dull on their own, but the environment you watched it in really elevated the movie.

The callbacks to earlier Tron films were handled in a way that felt thoughtful and satisfying without overshadowing the new direction. You can sense elements from the previous entries woven into this one, but the movie never leans so hard into nostalgia that it stops being its own thing. All three films feel like separate lanes connected by the same world, and Ares continues that pattern in a way that respects both the past and whatever the future of the franchise might be.

It is far from a perfect movie, but once everything wraps together, you understand what it was aiming for, and it leaves you more curious about what may come next. It is a fun, vibey sci-fi ride that works best if you go in wanting an experience instead of a flawless narrative.

It is the rare sequel that genuinely improves once you understand the first one, and the ending makes the whole journey feel more complete. It also becomes a film you want to revisit, because you know the second watch will hit differently.

title: After the Hunt
review:
After the Hunt sits in the psychological-thriller lane where nothing is clear, everything feels loaded, and you are forced to sit inside someone else’s emotional fog. The movie taps into themes that hit close to home in today’s world: trauma responses, trust, perception, and the thin line between what feels real and what actually is. It enters the cultural conversation about mental health, hidden pain, and how relationships bend under internal pressure.

The experience is trippy, confusing, and filled with signals you are constantly trying to interpret. The film throws distractions, hints, emotional swings, and shifting loyalties in a way that mirrors the protagonist’s inner world. You can never fully tell who is trustworthy, who is spiraling, or what version of reality the characters are operating in, and that confusion becomes part of the tension.

What grounds the story is the relationship at its center. The partner who stays steady becomes the emotional anchor, especially in the way he understands her trauma and refuses to take her spirals personally. Most people would crumble under that pressure, but he holds firm in a way that feels rare and deeply human.

There are moments that feel painfully familiar to real life. Times when someone carries their pain alone, thinking they deserve it. Times when trust collapses under stress. Times when you question what’s true, what’s distorted, and what’s fear-driven. And while the movie is chaotic, that chaos reflects how messy trauma actually is.

It’s a film with so much happening beneath the surface that it almost demands a rewatch. You leave knowing you missed details, clues, and emotional signals, unsure which parts were symbolic or literal.
