title: Good Fortune
review:
Good Fortune is one of those warm, feel-good movies Hollywood barely makes anymore. It’s simple, it’s sweet, and it hits that old-school charm lane without trying to be anything deeper than it is. And honestly, that’s why we enjoyed it.

Let’s be real: the acting is whatever. Seth Rogen is fun as always, but nothing in here is mind-blowing or award-worthy. The movie isn’t “good” in the technical, film-school sense at all. It’s kind of cheesy, kind of basic, and definitely not winning any craft points.

But that’s exactly the thing — we still liked it.

It’s refreshing to get a movie that’s just… good-hearted. No heavy message, no huge twists, no “look how smart we are” writing. Just a simple reminder to appreciate what you have, notice the small moments, and remember that your life is already full of good things if you slow down enough to see them.

The angel storyline adds a cute touch, nothing overly complex — just sweet. The comedy lands in that light, silly way that feels rare right now, and the whole thing kind of feels like a lost 2000s comfort movie.

Our score honestly comes from that feeling — not because the movie is objectively great, but because it’s nice to watch something harmless, positive, and warm for once.

title: Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere
review:
Deliver Me From Nowhere lands in that biopic space that focuses more on the emotional weight of a person’s life than the highlight moments of their career. It follows Bruce Springsteen from a lens that feels raw, personal, and heavy, choosing to explore the shadows that shaped him instead of the songs that defined him. It leans toward the quieter side of music storytelling, where the artist’s inner world takes center stage, even if that comes at the cost of understanding their art.

Watching it, the movie is fine. It is not a difficult watch, and the acting is strong across the board. It has emotional moments, thoughtful scenes, and a storyline that holds your attention. But it also doesn’t feel like it was made for everyone. If Springsteen wasn’t part of your era, your soundtrack, or your cultural upbringing, the movie ends up feeling more like an observation than an emotional connection. It is interesting, it is well-acted, but it doesn’t land as something personal.

One of the strongest elements is the relationship between Springsteen and his manager. Their loyalty and trust give the film its emotional core. Watching someone stand by him through his sadness, depression, and complicated emotional history is genuinely compelling. Those parts feel honest and grounded, even if the rest of the film feels distant. You get glimpses of a man who is hurting deeply, and someone behind the scenes who refuses to give up on him.

At the same time, the movie leaves a lot out. You do not walk away feeling like you learned anything meaningful about Springsteen’s music, songwriting, or evolution as an artist. It centers almost entirely on trauma from his childhood and how it shaped him, without balancing that perspective with the creative part of who he is. It feels more like one chapter of his life stretched across a full film rather than a fuller portrait. It is not bad — it just feels incomplete.

It is the kind of movie that longtime fans may respond to more deeply, but for others, it will feel like an interesting but distant experience. You can appreciate it, but you do not necessarily feel connected to it.

title: Shelby Oaks
review:
Shelby Oaks sits in the modern horror-thriller lane that blends mystery, internet culture, and emotional unraveling. It taps into the world of paranormal creators, missing-person investigations, and the kind of obsession that makes you question your own instincts. It leans more on atmosphere than jumps, building tension through uncertainty and emotional pressure.

The story pulls you into one woman’s desperation as she searches for her missing sister, convinced against all reason that she is still alive. You feel her obsession becoming its own gravity. You also feel the frustration from the people around her, who are torn between supporting her and wanting her to let go. The movie keeps you stuck between believing her intuition and doubting her completely, which becomes the core of the tension.

There are moments that feel unrealistic in that classic horror way where you think no one would stay in this situation. You catch yourself saying, I’d be out of here instantly. But the film sets those choices up for a reason. You watch from one lens for most of the movie, and then there is a single reveal that shifts everything you thought you were watching. It is the pump fake without warning — one of those perspective flips where everything you questioned earlier suddenly feels different.

The emotional payoff is what makes the film work. The final stretch reframes the entire journey, giving weight to moments that felt scattered before. Even if the middle drags or the pacing wobbles, the ending makes you appreciate the build-up in a stronger way.

For horror fans, it is absolutely worth watching. It is a solid, interesting thriller with a payoff strong enough to make you say damn when you finally see it all unfold in front of you.

title: Regretting You
review:
Regretting You fits into that nostalgic romance-drama lane that used to dominate the early 2000s. It has the same DNA as the classic book-to-film love stories that used to sweep people up with emotional arcs, tearjerker moments, and characters who grow through chaos. In a world full of noisy blockbusters, this feels like one of those calm, heartfelt films that gives you space to breathe and just feel something human.

It is a sad movie, but in a grounded way. The situations are dramatic, but believable enough that you can see how easily life could line up this way for real people. Families colliding, timing falling apart, people meant for each other drifting in and out of alignment, and new love showing up right when someone needs it most. The film sits in that emotional space where grief, romance, loyalty, and fate all overlap.

The love story between the girl and the boy is the highlight. Watching how long he has quietly been drawn to her, how everything finally lines up, and how naturally their story unfolds makes it feel poetic. There is something comforting about the way the movie shows timing working in the background, giving two people a chance that always felt slightly out of reach. It is unrealistic in some ways, but totally believable in others — the kind of romance that feels like it could absolutely happen in the real world if the universe nudged things just right.

The adults’ storyline also lands well, showing how people can be meant for each other even if life pushes them apart. The way they reconnect through tragedy has a softness to it that keeps the movie from feeling too dramatic. And the family dynamics feel real in the messy, painful way that families often are.

It ends up being one of those feel-good films that reminds you why people love romance stories in the first place. Emotional without being manipulative, dramatic without being over the top, and sweet without being cheesy.

title: Dream Eater
review:
Dream Eater sits in that dream-logic horror lane where reality is blurry, the rules keep shifting, and the scares come more from confusion and vibe than from big set pieces. It leans into the kind of trippy storytelling that keeps you wondering what is real, what is imagined, and what the hell is actually going on. It fits into the larger horror trend of ending with massive twists — the kind designed to flip your entire understanding of the movie in the last few minutes.

Watching it feels like drifting in and out of a nightmare. The movie is legitimately creepy, disorienting, and strange in a way that keeps you off balance. You even fell asleep a couple times, not because the film was bad, but because the vibe is hypnotic and you were just tired — and even then, the story still hit when you were awake. The twist at the end does exactly what modern horror loves to do: pull the rug out from under you in a wild, out-of-nowhere way that makes you think, damn, they really went for it.

There is also that classic horror logic gap where you find yourself yelling at the screen, wondering why the characters are still staying in these situations out of love or loyalty or denial. The movie pushes that tension hard — especially watching someone cling to a relationship far past the point where any normal person would dip. It raises that bigger question about the line between love, devotion, and simply ignoring danger. Some people see it as romantic, some see it as foolish, and horror movies tend to live in that uncomfortable middle.

As a whole, it is a good, freaky watch if you like twisty, trippy horror that scrambles your sense of reality. It is not the most profound film in the world, but it delivers the experience it promises and lands its final reveal in a way that sticks.

title: Violent Ends
review:
Violent Ends lives in the gritty crime-revenge lane where one decision spirals into the next until nobody can pull the brakes. It leans into the emotional weight behind violence, loyalty, ego, and the ways people get dragged back into worlds they are trying to escape. The film taps into that modern tragedy energy where every choice feels like it carries generational consequences, and where survival is tangled up with pride, fear, and desperation.

The story follows a man trying to live a clean life outside of his crime family, only to get pulled back in when everything he cares about is threatened. It is messy, emotional, frustrating, and full of those moments where you want to shake the characters because you can see how badly things will end if they keep choosing ego over common sense. You find yourself saying over and over, if they just took the deal, if they weren’t trying to be the toughest guy in the room, everything would have gone differently. Instead, everyone keeps doubling down until the worst-case scenario becomes inevitable.

The movie does a good job showing how violence spirals when fear and pride get involved. Every action feels like it is fueled by pain or panic, not logic. The villain energy is unsettling, the revenge beats are intense, and the emotional undertones hit harder than you expect. There is a real sadness beneath the action when you realize how avoidable so much of the story was, and how often real people destroy themselves for the same reasons.

It is not an extraordinary film, but it is a genuinely solid one. Entertaining, layered, emotional in unexpected places, and well-acted across the board. If you like revenge stories, crime families, or tragedies about masculinity imploding on itself, this is a good watch. If those themes annoy you, or you are tired of toxic masculinity as a genre engine, this one will feel heavy fast.

title: Bugonia
review:
Bugonia sits in the conspiracy-thriller lane where reality, delusion, and possibility blur together. It taps into the cultural moment where people argue about what’s real, what’s exaggerated, and what’s being hidden behind closed doors. The film leans into that tension, exploring political suspicion, corporate secrecy, family loyalty, and the way everyday people can get pulled into theories that feel wild but strangely familiar.

The story follows two cousins whose obsession with a powerful company spirals into something chaotic and strangely compelling. You watch them bounce between confidence and confusion, never fully sure whether they’re onto something or way off track. The movie never confirms anything outright. Instead, it taps into that real-world feeling where some people seem unhinged until their concerns stop sounding impossible. Not because the movie proves them right, but because it captures how modern paranoia grows out of just enough truth to keep you guessing.

There are a lot of layers underneath everything — family pressure, corporate greed, pharmaceutical mistrust, cultural tension, alien rumors, and the general sense that the world feels off. The film intentionally keeps things murky. It is ping-pong energy, constantly flipping between grounded realism and sci-fi intensity. Half the fun is not knowing what’s real, what’s exaggerated, and what’s just coincidence spiraling out of control.

The relationship between the cousins gives the movie its emotional anchor. Their loyalty, frustration, humor, and shared obsession keep the chaos grounded. Watching them feed into each other’s theories, argue, and try to protect one another makes every moment land with more weight.

Overall, Bugonia is a wild, layered, and surprisingly emotional ride. Not quite perfect, but easily one of the most interesting conspiracy-driven films of the year.

title: Vincent Must Die
review:
Vincent Must End sits in that offbeat thriller-comedy lane where a surreal, almost absurd premise is dropped into a world that otherwise feels completely normal. The movie plays with that tension — something horrific is happening, yet everyone around the main character reacts with an odd mix of disbelief, apathy, and shrugging acceptance. It creates a strange atmosphere where you cannot tell if the film is making a cultural point, a tonal joke, or simply leaning into the weirdness of its own universe.

At its core, the movie follows a man who suddenly becomes the target of random violence from strangers, and no one seems fazed by it except him. People don’t believe him, or they brush it off, or they act like it’s not that serious. That disconnect is where most of the tension comes from. You keep thinking, in the U.S. this would be a whole different story — lawsuits, outrage, viral videos, people losing their minds. But in this French setting, everything feels strangely low-stakes in the reactions, which becomes both unsettling and unintentionally funny. You’re stuck wondering whether that’s cultural, stylistic, or the film’s commentary on isolation and disbelief.

Narratively, it stretches itself a little long (like this review.. cough cough). There are stretches where you feel them delaying the inevitable just to prolong the question of how it’s all going to end. And then the moment finally arrives… and the movie refuses to give you the payoff you spent the whole runtime expecting. It’s one of those films that seems entirely aware of what the audience wants and actively chooses not to deliver it. Not in a clever way — more in a “sorry, you’re not getting that” way.

There is something fascinating about the concept, though. The movie feels like a metaphor about being dismissed, ignored, or left alone to deal with a nightmare no one takes seriously. But it also has moments where the reactions are so casual they pull you out of the experience. You’re left unsure whether it’s intentional surrealism or just an odd creative choice.

It is interesting, weird, frustrating, and definitely memorable — but also uneven. You walk out saying, that was something, but I don’t know if it was good or if I just survived it.

title: Hallow Road
review:
A slow, unsettling crawl toward a truth you’re not ready for.

Hollow Road starts grounded, then quietly pulls the floor out from under you. Something terrible has already happened, and the film forces you to piece it together through tension, fragments, and emotional unraveling rather than spectacle. It’s a long, anxious drive where every mile feels heavier than the last.

The pacing is intentionally uncomfortable. Much of the film plays like a near real-time journey, trapping you inside the car with two parents as they panic, argue, blame themselves, comfort each other, and spiral. At times it feels too long — but that stretch becomes part of the dread. Time, emotions, and reality all feel warped, and the movie uses that claustrophobia as a weapon.

What really works is the breadcrumb storytelling. Small details about the daughter drip out slowly, pushing you through cycles of empathy, frustration, guilt, and confusion. You feel for the parents, get angry at them, then feel bad for judging them. It’s watching people try to understand their child while failing her in ways they don’t even realize.

Then the ending hits — reframing everything without giving you clean answers. You’re left with multiple explanations, all equally upsetting, wondering what was real, what was imagined, and whether anyone ever truly understood what was happening.

Messy while you’re watching it, but haunting once it lands. Not perfect — definitely memorable.

title: Anniversary
review:
Anniversary lives in that rare overlap of drama, social commentary, and psychological tension. It jumps across years to show how one event ripples through relationships, families, and entire communities. You watch people harden, soften, grow, and fracture as time moves on, shaped by things they never chose.

What starts as a relationship drama slowly mutates into something political, symbolic, surreal, and unsettling. At times it feels exaggerated, even ridiculous, the media attention, the book deals, the sudden “movement,” the fame. You catch yourself thinking, what is even happening?

Then the metaphor lands.

The film isn’t exaggerating. It’s reflecting.
Small moments become national events.
Private pain becomes public narrative.
Ordinary people become symbols.

Once that clicks, everything snaps into focus and the emotional weight hits hard. Anniversary becomes a sharp, layered look at how movements are born and how families get swallowed by the world’s projections.

title: If I Had Legs I’d Kick You
review:
If I Had Legs, I’d Kick You sits in the surreal-drama lane where you’re meant to feel more than you understand. It moves through discomfort, ambiguity, and small human disasters in a way that mirrors how life collapses when too many fractures stack up. The film blends grounded struggle with dreamlike uncertainty, pulling you into a world where nothing is neatly explained and every interpretation feels both right and wrong at the same time.

It watches like a stream of tense moments where people make decisions out of fear, confusion, exhaustion, and survival. You see a mother spiraling under pressure, a daughter fading in the background, strangers appearing with unclear intentions, and everyone slipping between clarity and delusion. The movie never tells you which version of events is true. Instead, it lets you sit in the discomfort of piecing together what you think is happening without ever confirming whether you’re right.

There is a real sadness underneath everything — the kind that comes from watching someone try their best in impossible situations, yet still fail to protect the people who depend on them. The film brings up questions about responsibility, trauma, neglect, hope, guilt, and how easily life can unravel when someone is drowning emotionally with nobody around them to pull them out. You feel the weight of choices, the weight of avoidance, the weight of love twisted by circumstance.

What makes the film wild is how much it leaves unanswered. You never fully know who to trust, what is hallucination versus reality, what certain characters symbolize, or what the final moments truly mean. It leaves you holding the pieces, deciding for yourself whether the ending is hopeful, tragic, symbolic, literal, or something in between. It forces you to confront the idea that life rarely gives clean explanations, and sometimes the story only exists to stir the questions inside you.

The acting sells it completely. You believe the world, even if you don’t understand it. And the final sequence lands with a mix of beauty and confusion that leaves you staring at the screen after the credits.

title: Die My Love
review:
This one drops you straight into a reality that feels familiar on the surface and deeply off-kilter underneath. It’s quiet, raw, unsettling, and strange in a way that isn’t trying to shock you — it just lets you sit inside a life that doesn’t line up, where something always feels a little wrong. It has that eerie slice-of-life energy where the world looks normal, but the emotional gravity is tilted.

It follows a woman navigating the aftermath of giving birth, and the film sits right in that uncomfortable space where you can’t tell what’s real, what’s imagined, and what’s slipping between the cracks. The tone is uneasy from the start — not loud or jump-scary, but psychologically disorienting. You can feel the weight of postpartum depression threaded through it, though the movie refuses to give you clean answers or a clear before/after. It’s ambiguous by design, and that’s part of what makes it so uncomfortable.

There’s a secondary character — a man she keeps encountering — who blurs the line between hallucination, obsession, and actual interaction. The film intentionally never clarifies whether these moments are real, imagined, symbolic, or some messy combination of all three. That ambiguity makes the story interesting but also makes you ask, “Wait, what is this even about?” It’s part art-film, part psychological spiral, part emotional portrait.

What does land is the acting. It’s excellent — grounded, committed, and honest enough to keep you watching even when the story gets confusing or abstract. The movie isn’t boring and it stays watchable the whole way through, but it also never stops feeling a little disturbing and uncomfortable. It’s messy in theme, but compelling in execution.

title: Now You See Me: Now You Don’t
review:
The third chapter in the Now You See Me series delivers exactly the kind of theatrical chaos the franchise is built on — glossy illusions, impossible set pieces, quick banter, and that familiar dance between “this is ridiculous” and “okay, that was kinda sick.” It dips into modern buzzwords like AI and crypto, but mostly stays in its own lane: shiny heist-magic with just enough mystery to keep you watching for the next reveal. The fun of it comes from the spectacle and the reunion of familiar faces, not necessarily the story underneath.

The experience itself is what you’d expect: dramatic magic tricks, weirdly believable-unbelievable stunts, and that signature franchise charm where you keep asking “how the hell did they do that?” even though you know the real answer is “don’t think too hard.” As a pure theatrical ride, it’s entertaining. As a movie-movie, the cracks definitely show.

There’s a whole plotline about a diamond that becomes the central object of the story, and it leans into the franchise’s silliest energy — mysterious villain with an accent, over-the-top stakes, cartoonish motivations. It’s not bad, it’s just… the same movie again. And that becomes the main sticking point. Three films in, you can really feel the repetition.

The final twist is exactly what the franchise always does: one big reveal that reframes everything and makes you go “ahhh okay.” It works, but it also leans on the same formula fans already know. If you came for originality, this isn’t the one. If you came for returning characters, flashy illusions, and a popcorn-friendly magic heist, you’re good.

It’s a fun watch — just not groundbreaking, and definitely not reinventing anything.

title: The Running Man
review:
This one started with rock-bottom expectations — especially since Glenn Powell isn’t exactly loved in your household — but it ended up being a lot better than expected. What looks like another cheesy, mass-produced “licensed media” money-grab actually lands with a decent storyline, solid pacing, and a couple of fun cameo-style characters that help round it out.

The movie sits in that weird but enjoyable hybrid lane: part action romp, part dark comedy, part commentary on how far people will go when the cameras are rolling. It has a dystopian energy that feels like Minority Report if it were rewritten as a satire, mixed with the chaotic spectacle of Gamer and the morally questionable DNA of real-world reality television. It leans into the idea that entire systems exist to exploit people — sometimes for entertainment, sometimes for profit, sometimes for both — and the film has fun skewering that.

What works best is the story’s emotional center. Beneath the chaos, it’s really about a man doing whatever it takes for his family, even if he isn’t the cleanest or most perfect person. The humor lands, the action is solid, and the movie has just enough bite to feel grounded without ever getting too heavy. It’s darker than expected in parts, but still accessible and entertaining from start to finish.

title: Keeper
review:
Keeper opens with a bold move — a moment that feels like pure foreshadowing. It shows you a destination before you even know the journey. You instinctively know it means something, but the how, when, and why stay completely out of reach. The movie almost tricks you into forgetting that opening thread… until it circles back in a way that suddenly stings.

From the very start, the film throws you into stylish confusion. Every frame is composed like a fever dream — gorgeous, detailed, and disorienting in a way that makes you lean in even harder. You’re unsteady, unsure, and weirdly hooked.

As the story unfolds, you’re piecing things together moment by moment. The tension sits in your stomach. The mystery builds. And once the film finally snaps shut, you realize it’s been nudging you toward something tragic and poetic the whole time.

The ending — without spoiling anything — hits with an emotional irony that lands hard. It ties back to the film’s earliest hints, looping into this bittersweet idea of a person being undone by the very thing that once made them feel alive. It’s the kind of circular tragedy that feels mythic, even if the movie never says it outright.

Keeper is messy in the way all fever-dream thrillers are, but that’s the appeal. Confusing, tense, hypnotic — and unexpectedly thoughtful in its final beat.

title: Rental Family
review:
Rental Family sits in that rare category of films that feel gentle on the surface but hit somewhere deep and human underneath. It explores loneliness, connection, and the strange roles people step into — both intentionally and accidentally — just to make it through life. What begins as an arrangement turns into something unexpectedly honest, proving that authenticity can grow even in artificial soil. The movie invites you to look at the way people drift past each other, the way we pretend, and the way we give pieces of ourselves without noticing. Sometimes the film makes you confront the part of yourself that gives too much; sometimes it reminds you that you always have the right to choose differently. And at its core, it suggests a simple truth: you don’t always have to let people walk away emotionally. You can stop them. You can say something. You can push for connection instead of accepting distance.

Brendan Fraser is the heartbeat of this film.
He does an outstanding job grounding everything — warm, vulnerable, fully believable. He makes you root for him so hard that even when he sacrifices himself for someone else, you almost wish he’d been selfish for once. That’s how much the movie makes you want happiness for him. His performance adds weight to every moment and gives the film its emotional gravity.

The authenticity of the Japanese setting elevates everything. The culture, the city, the small details — none of it is watered down or Westernized. It feels real and intimate, like stepping into someone else’s world and recognizing pieces of your own humanity inside it.

title: Wicked: For Good
review:
Wicked: For Good is exactly what you’d expect from a second chapter, more spectacle, more emotion, more everything. It picks up cleanly from the first film and rarely drags, even if there are moments that feel indulgent. You can feel the ambition in every frame — massive sets, elaborate costumes, heavy production value — this movie clearly isn’t cutting corners.

That said, not all expansions feel necessary. Some time is spent deepening Glinda’s world in ways that feel less urgent than other threads that could’ve used more attention. There are moments where you wish the story stayed tighter, or shifted focus to characters and dynamics that feel more central to the emotional core. A few musical numbers and scenes feel like padding rather than propulsion.

Where the film shines is in craft. The makeup and costume work, especially for the Tin Man and Scarecrow, is genuinely impressive. The performances are strong across the board, and the cast clearly has the vocal power to carry a story this theatrical. Even when the pacing wobbles, it remains easy to watch and consistently entertaining.

Compared to the first installment, this one doesn’t hit quite as hard emotionally. The songs don’t linger in the same way, and some of the magic feels more manufactured than discovered. Still, as part two of a larger arc, it does its job — advancing the story, raising the stakes, and setting up what comes next.

More than anything, it leaves you curious. Not just about how Wicked ends, but about what Hollywood plans to do with this universe. Will they respect the existing material and deeper lore, or stretch it thin for the sake of more sequels? That question lingers as much as the story itself.

title: Zootopia 2
review:
Zootopia 2 drops you back into a world that’s easy to enjoy on a surface level. Animals living everyday lives, cops and civilians, jokes built on species stereotypes — it’s colorful, friendly, and familiar. What stands out most is the craftsmanship rather than the story. The animation is clean and polished, the world feels lived-in, and there are plenty of small visual jokes and references that reward paying attention. At the same time, nothing really demands your attention. The plot doesn’t linger, the emotional beats don’t hit particularly hard, and the story never quite rises above “pleasant.” It’s not pushing themes aggressively or trying to be overly allegorical — it mostly just lets the characters exist and move through a light, safe narrative.

That’s not a bad thing, especially for families. Kids will likely love it, and it’s an easy, comfortable theater watch. But as an adult viewer, it doesn’t give you much reason to revisit it or think about it afterward. It’s enjoyable in the moment, then fades.

The fox-and-bunny dynamic is still charming, Jason Bateman is still funny, and the world is still cute — it just doesn’t add much beyond that. Solid, watchable, and ultimately forgettable.

title: Eternity
review:
Eternity is a quiet, beautiful meditation on life, death, and the strange emotional limbo that comes after loss. It explores a situation most people recognize in some form — loving someone deeply, losing them, and then spending years wondering what might have been, even as life keeps offering beauty and connection. The film lives in that in-between space where grief, love, and doubt overlap.

What makes the movie resonate is how gentle it is. It doesn’t rush its ideas or force big emotional beats. Instead, it lets the story breathe, asking what it means to move forward when part of you is still looking backward. You can be surrounded by beauty, by good people, by a life that technically makes sense — and still feel uncertain. Still question. Still wonder.

The film leans into the idea that doing nothing can sometimes be just as impactful as making a choice. That if you don’t act, don’t speak, don’t take the risk for someone you love, entire lives can shift because of it. At the same time, it holds space for survival — for the slow, imperfect process of letting go, even when letting go takes years.

The performances elevate everything. Miles Teller brings a quiet wisdom that makes his character feel lived-in and reflective, while Callum Turner captures that restless, romantic uncertainty of your twenties, where everything feels fragile and possible at the same time. Together, they give the story emotional balance across time.

Visually, the film is calm and lovely, matching its themes. It’s not flashy. It’s reflective. It’s the kind of movie that lingers afterward — not because it shocks you, but because it gently asks you something personal.

title: Sisu: Road to Revenge
review:
Sisu: Road to Revenge lives in that stripped-down, mythic lane of action cinema — less plot, more momentum. It plays like a brutal, Rated-M adventure serial, where survival itself is the story and escalation is the language. You’re not here for exposition, you’re here to watch a force of nature keep moving forward.

What really locks it in is how physical everything feels. Every hit leaves a mark. Every crash costs something. The movie refuses that glossy, consequence-free action logic and instead leans into wear, damage, and exhaustion. You believe the pain, even as the situations get more extreme. That realism gives the film its edge.

The near-silence of the main character becomes a feature, not a bug. This isn’t about speeches or backstory — it’s about resolve. The bond with the dog quietly humanizes him, grounding the carnage in something simple and instinctive. That relationship does more emotional work than any monologue could.

At the same time, if relentless action isn’t your thing, this won’t convert you. The movie knows exactly what it is and never tries to broaden its appeal. It’s violent, graphic, and unapologetically singular. For some, that’s the whole draw. For others, it’s just too much of the same note.

Still, as an action experience, it’s undeniably effective. A lean, vicious survival tale that commits fully to its premise and doesn’t blink.

title: Fackham Hall
review:
Fackham Hall sits firmly in that loud, exaggerated comedy lane — the kind that doesn’t ask you to think, just to accept the bit and ride with it. It leans into broad English humor, physical gags, repeated jokes, and intentionally dumb punchlines that feel closer to Naked Gun or National Lampoon than anything modern or subtle.

The movie has a strange rhythm of highs and lows. Some jokes land clean, others drag or feel overplayed, but the pacing keeps it from feeling totally flat. There are enough twists and unexpected turns to stop it from becoming background noise, even if the humor itself isn’t particularly clever or sharp.

The cast does a lot of the heavy lifting. Recognizable British actors help sell jokes that otherwise might fall apart, giving the movie just enough momentum to stay watchable. It’s the kind of thing you’d throw on casually, not something you’re dissecting afterward.

Tonally, it feels Gen-Z coded with splashes of millennial and older-school comedy DNA. That mix won’t work for everyone. There are moments where it’s knowingly stupid in a fun way, and others where it’s just… stupid. Whether that works depends entirely on your tolerance for absurd, in-your-face humor.

At the end of the day, Fackham Hall knows what it is. It’s light, silly, occasionally surprising, and totally disposable — which, honestly, might be exactly what it’s aiming for.

title: Elf
review:
There’s a reason Elf has quietly cemented itself as a yearly ritual instead of just another Christmas movie. It doesn’t overreach, it doesn’t try to be clever about its sentiment, and it never apologizes for its silliness. It knows exactly what lane it’s in — warmth, belief, absurdity, and heart — and it commits fully.

Watching it in a theater only reinforces how well it’s built. The comedy hits harder when you’re locked in, the New York sequences feel alive because they are alive, and the world-building lands without feeling artificial or glossy. It’s goofy, but grounded just enough to feel real. That balance is rare.

What really carries the movie is how effortless it feels. The humor never becomes mean, the emotional beats never feel forced, and the fantasy is treated with sincerity instead of irony. The journey itself — believing, choosing joy, leaning into the impossible — is the point, and the film trusts that’s enough.

It also quietly gives its supporting characters space to grow. Watching reserved, closed-off people soften and step into belief alongside Buddy is part of why the movie sticks. It’s not heavy-handed, it’s just kind.
If there’s any nitpick at all, it’s a small one — but it doesn’t matter. Elf isn’t here to be dissected. It’s here to be felt, laughed with, and replayed every December without hesitation.

title: 100 Nights of Hero
review:
Going into this, it’s easy to think you know what you’re about to get. The trailers frame it like a stylized romance, almost a flipped “chick flick,” playing with desire, gender roles, and old-world fantasy tropes. That surface layer is there, but it’s not what the movie is actually about.

What makes 100 Nights of Hero so compelling is how quickly it reveals its depth. Beneath the romantic framing is a layered story about belief systems, power, sacrifice, and the way societies justify themselves because “that’s how it’s always been.” The fantasy world feels ancient, but the conversations, conflicts, and hypocrisies feel extremely modern. At times you’re watching it thinking this is ridiculous, then realizing how uncomfortably close it is to real life.

The film weaves forbidden love, constructed religion, social obedience, and quiet rebellion without ever feeling boring. Even when it gets a little cheesy, it stays cohesive. The pacing keeps you engaged, and you’re constantly reassessing what kind of movie you’re watching. It doesn’t spoon-feed its ideas, it lets them build until they start clicking.

One thing that really worked is how the performances are used. Even with recognizable names, no one feels like a cameo. Presence matters more than screen time, and the characters linger with you because of how they’re threaded through the story.

There’s something powerful about watching characters who aren’t trying to win or outsmart the system, but live honestly inside it, even when that honesty comes at a cost. By the time the story comes full circle, what started as a stylized fantasy feels intimate and earned.

This is one of those movies that might confuse you for a few minutes if you go in blind, but once you lock into its rhythm, it’s deeply engaging. It’s thoughtful without being pretentious, romantic without being shallow, and provocative without being loud.

title: Silent Night, Deadly Night
review:
On the surface, this looks like just another holiday slasher — killer Santa, cheap shocks, seasonal gimmick. At first, it honestly feels like that too. You’re watching it thinking, okay, here we go, another Christmas kill movie, and expecting nothing more than surface-level carnage.

But as the story unfolds, it starts to shift. The movie quietly reframes itself into something more tragic and strange. Instead of just leaning into shock value, it builds a character who’s been dealt a genuinely brutal hand in life — trauma stacked on trauma — and tries, in his own warped way, to make sense of it. What begins as violence starts to feel like a curse he’s struggling to live with rather than pure evil.

That’s where the movie becomes unexpectedly compelling. You’re not just watching kills anymore — you’re watching someone trying to impose order, balance, and meaning onto a world that taught him cruelty early and often. The film leans into a twisted moral framework, almost like a grim fairy tale or a dark Robin Hood fantasy, where “punishment” is aimed at wrongdoing. It’s uncomfortable, but intentional.

By the end, you realize the movie pulled off something risky: it gets you rooting for the killer. Not because the violence is justified, but because the humanity underneath it is visible. That tension — between empathy and horror — is what makes the film stick longer than expected. What starts as dismissible ends up surprisingly engaging, and even emotionally grounded in its own warped logic.

It’s not perfect, and it’s not subtle — but it’s far more thoughtful than its reputation suggests. By the final act, it hooks you enough that you’re genuinely curious where the story goes next.

title: Ella McCay
review:

The problems at the center of the story feel oddly small for how seriously they’re treated, and the stakes never rise enough to pull you in emotionally. It’s the kind of movie you sit through without leaving, then never think about again.

The cast is stacked — Woody Harrelson, Jamie Lee Curtis, Kumail Nanjiani — which almost makes it more confusing. There are moments where you can tell talented people are trying, but the material gives them very little to work with. Instead of sharpening the story, the performances just highlight how thin it all feels.

Tonally, it lands in an awkward middle space. It wants to feel important, but never earns it. It wants to say something about power, image, and personal fallout, but the issues presented rarely feel consequential outside of this very specific bubble.

By the end, there’s no emotional hook, no lingering idea, and no reason to revisit it. Not disastrous — just empty.

title: Song Sung Blue
review:
Song Sung Blue sits in that familiar musical-biopic-adjacent lane — a story about passion, struggle, love, and persistence, framed through music that clearly means a lot to someone, just not necessarily to us. You can feel the intention behind it: perseverance, finding joy in the work, and continuing on even when life keeps throwing punches.

The movie isn’t bad. In fact, it’s solidly made. Hugh Jackman and Kate Hudson both do good work, and there are moments where the emotional weight almost pulls you in. The story gets heavy, sometimes uncomfortably so, and while that’s honest, it also makes it hard to fully root for the characters. They’re flawed in very real ways, but not always in ways that invite empathy.

Structurally, the film tries to juggle a lot at once — music, romance, addiction, tragedy, ambition — and while none of it is poorly executed, it does feel crowded. Instead of one clear emotional throughline, it’s more like a series of hardships stacked together, which can be draining rather than moving.

Where it does succeed is in its ending. There’s a quiet message about not giving up, about continuing to show up for your life even when it’s messy or disappointing. That resolution softens the experience and reframes the sadness into something gentler and more hopeful.

Ultimately, this is a movie that will work much better if you’re already invested in the genre, the music, or the spirit of musical dramas. For everyone else, it’s respectful, competent, and emotionally sincere — just not especially compelling.

title: Dust Bunny
review:
Dust Bunny immediately signals that it’s not playing by normal rules. It’s highly stylized, surreal, and intentionally disorienting — the kind of movie where you’re not supposed to fully understand what’s happening so much as feel your way through it. Reality, imagination, and symbolism blur together almost instantly.

At its core, the movie leans on the strange relationship between the young protagonist and her odd little companion. That dynamic is where most of the charm lives. There’s something endearing there, even when the movie itself feels chaotic or childish in a way that’s hard to pin down. It almost plays like a story invented by a kid — imaginative, messy, and driven by emotion rather than logic.

That said, the tone is confusing in a way that doesn’t always feel intentional. The film feels like it might be for children, but also feels like something you absolutely shouldn’t show a child. It’s creepy without being scary, whimsical without being comforting, and strange without always being compelling. You’re left wondering who exactly the movie is made for.

There are flashes of action and creativity, and the Dust Bunny itself is undeniably cute, but the film never fully commits to being thrilling, meaningful, or emotionally grounded. It ends up feeling more like an art experiment than a fully realized story — interesting to experience, but not especially satisfying.

title: Avatar: Fire and Ash
review:
There’s no denying it — Avatar: Fire and Ash is stunning to look at. The scale, the color, the world-building craft are all dialed all the way up. There are moments that genuinely make you stop and think, yeah, that’s sick. James Cameron still knows how to create spectacle better than almost anyone alive.

But once the awe wears off, you start to feel the weight of something missing. The movie feels less like a new chapter and more like a remix of what we’ve already seen. It leans hard into expanding the world, introducing new factions and environments, but without giving the story enough momentum to justify its length. It often feels like you’re watching part two again, just with different lighting and terrain.

There are flashes of humor and a few playful, cheeky moments that almost wake the movie up, but they never fully land. Even the most memorable sequences feel like they could’ve gone harder. The emotional beats don’t stick, the stakes feel oddly distant, and the narrative rhythm drags — to the point where you start wondering who this is really for. Kids might find it long. Adults might find it hollow. Hardcore fans might appreciate the lore, but even that starts to feel repetitive.

From a storytelling standpoint, it’s frustrating. You can feel the intention to say something bigger — about division, conflict, identity — but it never crystallizes into anything compelling. Instead, it circles familiar ground without offering a fresh perspective. The result is a movie that’s technically impressive but surprisingly dull to sit through.

title: The Housemaid
review:
At first, The Housemaid feels like it’s playing a familiar game. You think you know the type of movie you’re watching. The setup feels obvious, the clues feel intentional, and for a while it almost dares you to get ahead of it. That early stretch can feel long, even frustrating, like it’s leaning too hard into something you’ve already seen before.

But then the movie starts shifting. Slowly. Uncomfortably. What initially feels straightforward begins to splinter, and once it does, it doesn’t stop. The film turns into a psychological pressure cooker where every character starts revealing different sides of themselves, and your sense of who to trust keeps changing. You’re constantly reassessing — the parents, the child, the relationships, the power dynamics — all of it.

What really works is how the movie never lets you settle. Just when you think you’ve figured out the angle, it pivots again. It keeps pulling you left and right, forcing you to sit in that uneasy space where nothing feels clean or justified, even when characters try to justify themselves. There’s a deep, lingering toxicity baked into every layer — wealth, family, control, silence — and the film doesn’t let you look away from it.

By the end, you’re left with an uncomfortable feeling that doesn’t resolve neatly. Even when things “wrap up,” it still feels wrong — and that’s clearly the point. The open-endedness isn’t about answers, it’s about sitting with the damage, the choices people made, and the things society is willing to ignore when status and money are involved.

It’s a movie that rewards patience. If you stick through the slower, predictable beginning, what follows is tense, absorbing, and unsettling in a way that lingers well after the credits roll.

title: Not Without Hope
review:
Movies based on true events always carry extra weight, especially when they deal with survival. Not Without Hope drops you into a situation that’s immediately uncomfortable because you know this really happened. There’s no escapism here, no fantasy buffer. Just people, water, and the reality that things can go wrong fast.

From the jump, the film keeps you engaged. There aren’t many dull moments, but it’s not because it’s exciting in a fun way — it’s because it makes you feel trapped with them. The camera work plays a huge role in that. The way the lens moves through the water, the moments where visibility drops, even the water hitting the camera itself, all make it feel like you’re right there instead of watching safely from a distance.

Emotionally, it’s a tough sit. You feel helpless watching decisions stack on top of each other, knowing none of it is going to end cleanly. Not in a “what happens next?” way, but in a “this is bigger than them” way. The ocean doesn’t care. That’s the quiet terror underneath the whole movie — how small people really are when nature takes control.

What grounds the film is the bond between the friends. At its core, this isn’t just a survival story, it’s about loyalty, perseverance, and refusing to give up on each other even when the odds are completely unfair. It’s also a reminder of how one or two seemingly minor choices can become catastrophic when the environment turns hostile.

Watching it in a theater feels almost surreal. You’re sitting there with snacks and comfort while the story unfolding is anything but comfortable. It leaves you reflective rather than entertained — about risk, about loved ones, and about how fragile control really is.

title: Hamnet
review:
This is one of those movies that feels less like something you watch and more like something you sit inside. Hamnet is emotionally dense, layered, and heavy in a way that’s intentional — not for shock, not for spectacle, but for truth. It carries the weight of loss, creativity, memory, and the quiet ways people survive after something shattering.

What hits hardest is how many perspectives the film holds at once. Every character is on their own grief journey, reacting differently, coping differently, sometimes selfishly — but with purpose. Not vanity, not cruelty, just people doing what they can to keep going. The film makes space for that complexity without judging it.

There’s a powerful idea running through the story: grief can be creative. Loss doesn’t just hollow people out — it reshapes them. It can give new life to things that were never lived, let the dead exist in other forms, other experiences. That concept alone carries the movie far beyond a simple historical drama and into something much more universal.

Some moments are intentionally difficult. Dialogue can be hard to catch. Certain sequences — especially when the story moves toward art itself — feel disorienting or opaque. But the emotion never gets lost. Even when you’re not fully tracking every word, you feel what’s happening. And that feeling lingers.

This isn’t a movie you casually throw on. It demands attention, patience, and emotional openness. But if you give it that, it rewards you with something rare — a story that acts like a mirror, a portal, and a quiet reckoning all at once.

title: We Bury the Dead
review:
We Bury the Dead is an interesting take on the zombie genre — not because it reinvents the apocalypse, but because it barely seems interested in it. This isn’t really about the undead. It’s about obsession, denial, and the idea that love can survive anything… even when it probably shouldn’t.

The movie follows a woman traveling through a broken world to find her husband. On paper, that’s compelling. Of course you’d cross hell for your partner. That instinct is universal. But as the journey drags on, the movie starts to feel thin. You’re watching her push forward endlessly, and you keep waiting for the story to give that drive more urgency, more meaning, more fire.

When the emotional truth finally surfaces — the infidelity, the already-fractured relationship, the idea that both of them were broken before the world ever ended — it reframes everything in a darker, more uncomfortable way. Suddenly the quest feels less romantic and more desperate. Less love story, more refusal to accept what was already dead.

There are moments that work. A few tense scenes land. The acting is solid and grounded. The movie doesn’t overstay its welcome, which honestly helps a lot. It gets in, tells its story, and gets out without drowning itself in melodrama.

But by the end, it still feels like a missed opportunity. The premise had room to go harder, emotionally and narratively. Instead, it settles into something that’s watchable, occasionally engaging, but ultimately a little empty — like chasing closure that was never going to fix anything anyway.

title: Marty Supreme
review:
Marty Supreme arrived with a ton of hype, and honestly, it mostly earns it. It’s a long movie, but it stays engaging the entire time, constantly moving, constantly connecting dots. Nothing feels wasted. By the end, everything is tied together cleanly, which is rare for a film this ambitious.

At the center is Marty himself — not an easy character to love. He’s selfish, ambitious to a fault, and more than willing to step on people if it gets him closer to what he wants. And yet, you still root for him. That’s the magic trick of the movie. It understands that passion and ego often live side by side, and that pursuing a dream sometimes means disappointing people you care about — or choosing yourself when it hurts others.

Timothée Chalamet absolutely commits. He makes Marty feel real, flawed, and human. You don’t excuse his behavior, but you understand it. The film quietly asks how much you’re willing to sacrifice to make yourself happy — and whether the version of success you imagine is actually the one you want when you finally reach it.

Visually and tonally, the period setting never feels dusty or distant. Even though it’s rooted in another era, the energy feels modern. The ambition, the competition, the obsession — all of it translates easily to now. The world feels alive, and the culture around Marty’s pursuit is oddly infectious. You leave the theater buzzing, wanting to talk about it, replaying scenes, questioning choices.

The ending lands in a deliberately ambiguous space. It doesn’t hand you a clean emotional answer. You’re left wondering what Marty’s tears really mean — relief, regret, acceptance, or something unfinished. That uncertainty feels intentional, and it fits the story. Dreams don’t always end the way we expect them to, even when we get close.

It’s messy, driven, entertaining, and quietly reflective. A movie about ambition that doesn’t pretend ambition is noble — just human.

title: Anaconda
review:
Anaconda plays like a playful throwback wrapped in modern comedy energy. At its core, it’s less about the snake and more about a group of childhood friends who drifted apart, stayed loosely connected, and somehow get pulled back together by a half-baked creative dream. Watching them stumble into the jungle to make this weird, homemade project is honestly part of the fun — it feels like grown-ups chasing a version of their younger selves.

The movie works best when it leans into that energy. There’s something genuinely enjoyable about seeing people relive old dreams, mess around, and pretend they’re still kids making something just because they want to. The comedy is hit-or-miss, very much in the Jack Black and Paul Rudd lane — some jokes land clean, some drag, some feel a little too slow — but when it works, it’s charming.

The pacing helps. It’s short, it doesn’t overstay its welcome, and the ending is easily the strongest part. By the final act, it almost feels like you’re wandering through a Hollywood backlot version of the jungle — playful, self-aware, and clearly not trying to be taken too seriously. The cameos and Easter eggs add to that fun, giving it a wink-and-nod energy that rewards paying attention.

That said, this movie lives and dies by its cast. Without Paul Rudd and Jack Black, it probably collapses. Their likability does a lot of heavy lifting, and they’re the main reason you stay engaged even when parts of the story fall flat. The snake itself feels a bit too exaggerated and cartoony, which pulls you out of it at times, especially if you were hoping for something more grounded or suspenseful.

Overall, it’s not amazing, but it’s easy. A light, silly watch that makes you smile more than it makes you think — and honestly, that’s kind of the point.

title: The Dutchman
review:
The Dutchman feels less like a traditional movie and more like a psychological stage play unfolding on screen. Everything is heightened — the dialogue, the pauses, the performances — in a way that constantly reminds you that what you’re watching is constructed, but intentionally so. It’s dramatic without being loud, theatrical without feeling fake.

What really pulls you in is the sense of temptation and slow unraveling. You’re hooked not because you fully understand what’s happening, but because you don’t. The movie speaks in riddles, references history and other works, and never quite explains who’s in on what — or if anyone is. That ambiguity becomes part of the tension. You’re always wondering: is this person real, symbolic, losing it, or guiding him somewhere darker?

There’s also something eerie about the setting. New York is usually overwhelming, crowded, alive — but here it feels empty, almost staged. Subway cars with no one else. Streets with no background noise. It adds to the feeling that this story exists slightly outside reality, like a liminal space where one bad decision can quietly snowball into something irreversible.

Emotionally, it’s a bit of a puzzle box. You don’t always know who’s spiraling, who’s manipulating, or whether the danger is external or entirely internal. Spirits? Demons? Metaphor? Or just a man cracking under pressure? The movie never gives you a clean answer, and that uncertainty is both its strength and its frustration.

If you’re familiar with the source material or the mythology behind “The Dutchman,” it probably clicks harder. If you’re not, it still works — just more as an unsettling experience than a clearly decoded message. It’s not spectacular in a crowd-pleasing way, but it is provocative, strange, and memorable in how it lingers.

title: The Plague
review:
The Plague drops you straight into the early-2000s headspace, the kind that instantly feels familiar if you grew up around it. There’s a strong nostalgic pull, not in a comforting way, but in a disorienting one. It captures an era where everything felt slightly off, blue-tinted, and emotionally confusing. You’re back in that in-between age where the world feels big, rumors feel dangerous, and reality isn’t always clear.

What makes the movie work is how it blurs lines. You’re never totally sure how much of what you’re watching is just kids being kids, bullying, posturing, trying to fit in, versus something darker and psychological underneath. Is it a thriller? A horror story? Or just a painfully honest slice of adolescence where fear and imagination feed each other? The film refuses to answer that cleanly, and that uncertainty becomes part of the experience.

There’s a constant feeling that you’re missing something, like there are messages just out of reach, details you didn’t catch, truths forming in the background. That mirrors being young, when you rarely have the full picture but still act as if you do. Even when you think you know what’s real, the movie drops small contradictions that make you second-guess yourself.

From a character standpoint, it avoids the nostalgic fantasy of boyhood. This isn’t The Sandlot. There’s no easy brotherhood. Instead, it’s about insecurity, social pressure, and how much boys shape their behavior around what others think. You watch the main character slowly change through subtle, uncomfortable shifts until by the end he’s not quite the same kid anymore.

The Plague isn’t always easy to follow, and that feels intentional. It’s meant to feel overwhelming, confusing, and emotionally unsettled. But that discomfort is why it sticks. It captures growing up when you’re not sure if the danger is external… or something you’re creating yourself.

title: Is This Thing On?
review:
Is This Thing On? feels less like a movie and more like being dropped into someone’s life mid-sentence. It’s raw without being performative, funny without softening the blow, and emotionally honest to the point it almost feels intrusive, in the best way. You don’t realize it’s based on true events until the end, and once you do, everything hits harder in retrospect.

What makes it work is how alive it feels. The film never feels staged. Scenes breathe. Conversations overlap. People talk in the background. Imperfections stay in. It creates the feeling that you’re not watching actors hit marks, you’re watching real people exist, parents, kids, friends, partners, all moving through the same messy moment together. That looseness is the magic.

Will Arnett is incredible here. He grounds the movie with a performance that’s vulnerable, frustrated, self-aware, and deeply human. Bradley Cooper adds another layer, the dreamer, the screw-up, the guy who hasn’t quite figured it out but still believes there’s something more. Their dynamic, along with the bond between the couples, feels lived-in and authentic rather than written.

The comedy lands because it comes from truth. It’s funny the way real life is funny, uncomfortable, awkward, sometimes sad, sometimes absurd. And when the movie leans into heavier moments, it doesn’t overplay them. It lets them sit, trusting you to feel them without being told how.

At its core, this is a story about people falling apart, reconnecting, and choosing to live on their own terms instead of the ones they’re “supposed” to follow. It’s about relationships fraying and repairing, not having the answers, and finding meaning in the middle of the chaos.

Nothing about Is This Thing On? feels polished, and that’s exactly why it works. It’s imperfect, intimate, and deeply relatable. The kind of movie that sneaks up on you and stays with you long after it ends.

title: Primate
review:
Primate taps into a very real fear, the idea that an animal you can’t physically overpower suddenly turns on you. From the jump, it understands that monkeys aren’t cute chaos mascots, they’re strong, unpredictable, and terrifying when framed as a threat. The movie proves that and rarely lets up.

What makes the horror hit is how grounded it feels. This isn’t supernatural or mystical, it’s just a bad decision spiraling out of control. You spend most of the movie screaming internally at the characters to grab anything, a weapon, a phone, a plan, while knowing that fear freezes people in real life. That tension between “what you’d do” and “what panic looks like” drives the experience.

The monkey itself is the film’s secret weapon. Knowing it’s a performer in a suit instead of CGI makes it scarier. It moves wrong. It feels physical. There’s weight to it. It doesn’t feel like a movie monster, it feels like an unstoppable, ugly force that keeps coming. Every failed attempt makes things feel more hopeless.

Structurally, the movie is relentless. The pacing makes it feel like everything is happening in real time, all in one night, with no reset button and no daylight relief. The lack of heavy scoring works in its favor. Silence and sudden chaos do more than a manipulative soundtrack. When the violence hits, it hits fast and viciously.

Emotionally, it’s bleak as hell. Even when the core family survives, it doesn’t feel like a win. Everyone who tries to help dies, friends, outsiders, collateral damage, all gone. The movie doesn’t reward good intentions or bravery. It reinforces how cruel and unfair survival horror can be, and that toxicity feels intentional.

Primate isn’t trying to be elevated or metaphor-heavy. It’s a raw survival nightmare built on a fear that feels disturbingly plausible. If you hate horror because it feels fake or lazy, this one might surprise you. If you already hate monkeys… this will ruin you.

title: I Was a Stranger
review:
I Was a Stranger doesn’t feel like entertainment so much as witness. It drops you into the reality of people living through the Syrian conflict and refuses to soften it or make it palatable. Watching from a theater feels wrong at times, because every explosion, death, and decision carries the weight of knowing this isn’t metaphor, it’s lived experience.

What makes the film hit so hard is how personal it is. You’re not watching “a refugee crisis,” you’re following people, a doctor, a mother, a child, a smuggler, strangers who become a temporary family. Every character is layered. Even the morally gray ones aren’t villains, just people trying to survive, provide, or protect someone they love. There’s no clean heroism here, just endurance.

The journey is brutal. Crossing borders, navigating fear, trusting strangers, losing people along the way, it’s exhausting to watch. When the film jumps forward and shows where survival lands some of these people, it’s quietly devastating. Doctors become janitors. Professionals start over from nothing. Safety comes at the cost of identity, pride, and the life you once knew.

One of the most powerful elements is how community reappears in the darkest moments. People sharing what little they have. Strangers risking themselves. Volunteers and coast guards acting from humanity rather than obligation. The movie asks an unspoken question: if you were there, would you do any different?

The film forces you to confront how easily labels get thrown around, terrorist, criminal, threat, and how absurd they feel when you’re watching parents carry children through hell just to keep them alive. It’s uncomfortable, eye-opening, and humbling. The message is clear: empathy isn’t optional when survival is on the line.

This isn’t an easy watch. It’s sad, heavy, and overwhelming. But it’s also deeply human, necessary, and grounding. It doesn’t ask for pity. It asks for understanding.

title: Greenland 2: Migration
review:
Greenland 2: Migration is one of those disaster sequels that knows its lane and never really leaves it. Every beat feels familiar, the escape almost works, something explodes, they barely survive, repeat. After a while, the tension flattens because you see the pattern coming. It’s not bad, it’s just exhausting in a mechanical way.

The movie leans hard into movement, convoys, borders, checkpoints, survival logistics, and constant interruption. That nonstop almost-making-it energy should feel stressful, but instead it numbs you. At some point, you stop caring whether they arrive or not. Make it there, don’t make it there, either way feels fine, which isn’t great for a movie built on survival.

That said, it’s not a mess. Gerard Butler does exactly what he always does, grounding the chaos as a dad trying to keep his family alive. The performances are solid, the scale is big, and the destruction is impressive in that classic end-of-the-world way. Watching nature dismantle civilization is still fun, especially if you like “what if” scenarios and large-scale catastrophe.

What’s interesting is how hollow it feels next to something real. Coming off a film about actual displacement and survival, this one feels weightless. Similar ideas, families on the move, borders, desperation, but without emotional gravity. Even the deaths don’t land, not because they’re shocking, but because there’s no real attachment.

The one moment that does hit is the son’s arc. Watching him grow and finally honor his father feels earned, and it’s the closest the movie gets to something emotionally resonant. Beyond that, it’s mostly spectacle and repetition.

It’s not terrible. It’s not great. It’s fine. A solid disaster sequel that delivers exactly what you expect, and not much more.

title: 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple
review:
Zombie horror can offer plenty of brutality. Finding something beautiful inside it is harder. The Bone Temple does both, delivering a continuation that feels unpredictable, disturbing, and surprisingly full of life.

Two stories unfold and collide without feeling like another familiar trip through the same world. There are moments when the characters become so absorbing that you almost forget you’re watching a zombie movie. Then something deeply unsettling happens, or something makes you laugh, and you remember how strange this whole experience is. Hilarious and disturbing is a difficult combination to pull off. This one gets there.

Ralph Fiennes is the standout. The doctor’s connection with Samson gives the film an unexpected tenderness, making room for something beyond the threat of another monster. Those scenes were among the most compelling parts of the movie—strange, beautiful, and genuinely exciting to watch.

The connection between the younger characters gives the chaos another emotional anchor. There’s something worth caring about in how they find each other and offer protection inside such an ugly world. Add the gorgeous cinematography, striking shots, and an ending that leaves you buzzing, and the whole thing feels alive with possibility.

Holy fuck, this was a fantastic surprise. It left us wanting to watch it again and excited to see where this world goes next.

title: Dead Man’s Wire
review:
Dead Man’s Wire finds an entertaining rhythm inside a serious situation. The tension is there, but so are moments of playfulness and unexpected relaxation. The music carries a lot of that contrast, giving a movie built around one hostage standoff more personality than the setup might suggest.

The lead performance keeps it compelling. There’s something interesting about watching someone who feels unstable without seeming eager to become a killer. That uncertainty makes him sympathetic enough to follow, even as the situation gets further out of hand.

The radio DJ is another standout, and the reporter’s storyline adds welcome depth beyond the immediate confrontation. Those different angles help keep the movie engaging. It never became boring, but they also hint at how much more there might have been to explore.

That’s the main frustration: the film stays so close to the standoff that the life surrounding it can feel just out of reach. More of what brought him there—how he felt screwed over, pieces of his past, another perspective—could have given the story greater range. Staying tightly focused is an interesting choice; it just leaves you wanting another layer.

The real footage afterward makes the portrayal feel especially convincing. It’s an unbelievable story, carried by strong performances and a soundtrack that knows how to play against the tension. An enjoyable watch, with enough going for it to make you wish it had opened its world a little wider.

title: The Choral
review:
There’s something quietly sad about people building a life together while a war keeps pulling it apart. The Choral finds beauty, humor, and warmth in that space, following a group whose shared purpose becomes harder to hold onto as the world changes around them.

The pleasure is often in the people. The central character’s personality and the way he runs things give the film energy, while the younger characters and those connected to the army bring entertaining moments of their own. The bikes, outfits, and sets make the period setting enjoyable to spend time in, with different lives unfolding around the choir.

Watching the group improve gives the story a satisfying progression. The singing can be beautiful, and it avoids the cheesiness that sometimes makes musicals difficult to settle into. But those performances also slow the film down. There’s a lot to appreciate without every musical stretch being equally absorbing, and the running time starts to make itself felt.

What gives the movie weight is the gradual loss of the people bringing those voices together. The story comes full circle in a way that feels sad rather than reassuring. People try to be patriotic and keep something meaningful alive, while having very little say in what happens to them.

That feeling—being a pawn in a much bigger game—lingers beyond the music. A worthwhile watch with heartfelt and funny moments, even if its slower passages keep it from landing more strongly.

title: No Other Choice
review:
Providing for your family sounds like a reason almost anyone can understand. No Other Choice takes that instinct somewhere deeply uncomfortable, making you root for a man while questioning how much you’re willing to excuse just because you understand what he wants.

It’s funny, absorbing, and full of interesting characters. The situations keep unfolding in ways that make it easy to follow someone who is clearly getting in over his head. Even the length feels earned. There wasn’t a stretch that seemed disposable, and the story flows well enough that the subtitles become part of the experience rather than an obstacle.

A little more time inside some of the other characters’ lives would have been welcome. There’s plenty happening around this man’s pursuit, and those glimpses are interesting enough to leave you curious. Still, the movie keeps its focus and holds your attention.

The uncomfortable part is how familiar his sense of desperation can feel. Sometimes wanting something badly enough makes every alternative seem impossible. You stop asking whether the goal is worth it and start treating anything in the way as something to overcome. But if getting there means making everyone around you suffer, maybe what needs to change is the thing you’re chasing.

That’s the bitter pill. The movie makes his pursuit entertaining without making it easy to feel good about. You can understand the pressure, enjoy the humor, and still find yourself thinking: hold on, what the fuck am I rooting for?

A really good film that keeps you engaged in the moment and leaves the harder questions waiting afterward.

title: Night Patrol
review:
Night Patrol looks like it’s heading down a familiar road: cops, gang violence, and a situation you can already imagine ending badly. Then it takes a turn that makes the whole thing more playful—and more entertaining—than the trailer suggested.

That surprise does a lot for the movie. There’s real-world ugliness underneath the setup, but the film twists it into something stranger, keeping you guessing about what might happen next. Going in expecting a straightforward cop movie makes that change of direction especially enjoyable.

The pacing doesn’t always keep up with the chaos. Some stretches drag, and the cheesiness can be hard to miss. Still, the performances bring enough fun and playfulness to keep it from becoming a dull watch. It has slow parts without losing all its energy.

Justin Long’s character is harder to get a read on. He seems positioned as a good cop while continuing to do shady shit, and the movie doesn’t always make that contradiction convincing. Is he conflicted? Trying to do better? Just another bad guy? There’s room for that uncertainty to be interesting, but here it can feel more confusing than compelling.

What carries Night Patrol is its willingness to take the familiar setup somewhere unexpected. Messy in places, uneven in its momentum, but entertaining enough to make the surprise worthwhile. More fun than expected, even when it doesn’t quite make sense.

title: The Fire Raven
review:
The Fire Raven packs action, mystery, thriller tension, and some nasty violence into a story that keeps you busy figuring out who’s who and what the hell is happening. It’s creative, occasionally goofy, and a little cheesy—but there’s enough going on to make the ride entertaining.

The brother-and-sister relationship gives that chaos something to hold onto. Beneath the shifting suspicions and competing storylines, the family connections are what make the movie land. The emotional weight becomes clearer as the pieces come together, giving the mystery more than just another answer to chase.

Following those pieces can take some work. With so much happening onscreen, reading the subtitles sometimes means missing a look, a detail, or part of the action. The broad strokes are easy enough to follow, but keeping track of everyone’s role can feel like playing catch-up. By the end, earlier moments start clicking into place.

There’s fun in trying to get ahead of it, too. After enough mysteries, you start recognizing when a movie is steering you toward someone suspicious. You think you’ve caught the trick—until it sends you somewhere else. That guessing game helps keep this one engaging.

The ending stretches that patience a little. It reaches what feels like a stopping point, then adds another piece, then another. Those extra beats help bring things together, but they also make the finish feel drawn out. And the gore can be a bit much, even when the action is otherwise enjoyable.

Still, the family story gives the spectacle a feeling that lasts beyond the mystery. Uneven, busy, and sometimes exhausting, but a good watch with an emotional payoff underneath all the moving parts.

title: Return to Silent Hill
review:
Return to Silent Hill feels like watching a video game unfold. It’s fun, scary, and intriguing, with enough going on beneath the surface to leave you thinking about how it all connects.

That game-like feeling defines the experience. It gives the movie a distinct appeal, even if the result lands somewhere between loving it and hating it. There’s something interesting here without it becoming a film you fully connect with.

The ending is what gives it more weight. The way it circles back around makes the story feel deeper, bringing you back to the intensity of that love and everything wrapped up in it. It’s the part that leaves you turning the movie over afterward.

A good flick with an intriguing finish—enjoyable enough, even if it never quite becomes a favorite.

title: Clika
review:
Clika finds its appeal in a dream that feels close to home: making music with your friends, building something for your family, and trying to turn what you love into a future. The struggles along the way give that ambition weight, but the movie keeps the experience fun and entertaining from beginning to end.

There’s a particular pleasure in seeing California communities and familiar places represented onscreen. The setting feels recognizable, and the Latin culture is a big part of what makes the film connect. You’re watching people pursue something meaningful in a world you can recognize, which makes it easier to get invested in where they’re headed.

The music, friendships, and family ties give that pursuit its appeal. Chasing a dream involves the people beside you as much as the person trying to make it happen, and that shared experience is what makes this an enjoyable watch.

The acting is uneven. Some characters feel less convincing than others, and those weaker performances stand out. Fortunately, the stronger ones do enough to carry the film through those moments without losing the connection that makes it work.

Clika leaves a good feeling. An entertaining story about ambition and the people you bring along with you, with a welcome sense of recognition for the culture and communities it puts onscreen.
