title: H Is for Hawk
review:
Grief can make the familiar world feel impossible to live in. H Is for Hawk approaches that feeling through Helen, who turns to training a goshawk after the sudden loss of her father. Their shared connection to birds becomes part of how she tries to navigate his absence.

There’s something compelling about seeking comfort in an animal that has no understanding of what you’ve lost. Mabel isn’t there to offer reassurance or explain how to move on. She’s a wild creature with needs of her own, giving Helen something immediate to focus on when everything else feels overwhelming.

That relationship opens up a simple, human idea: caring for something can give your days direction without making the pain disappear. Memory, nature, and the work of building a connection become ways of continuing to live alongside loss.

A story about finding something to hold onto when the person you want most is no longer there.

title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die
review:
Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die takes our relationship with technology to a ridiculous extreme, but the uncomfortable part is how much already feels familiar. The phones, the escape into virtual worlds, the promise of AI—it’s a satirical nightmare with enough truth underneath the chaos to make the jokes sting.

It’s also really fucking entertaining. The characters are interesting, the lead is easy to root for, and the story keeps finding ways to catch you off guard. For a movie dealing with such bleak possibilities, it has enough humor and unpredictability to keep the experience playful rather than crushing.

The technology itself isn’t the whole problem. There’s something exciting about tools that could connect people or open experiences they couldn’t otherwise access. The ugliness comes from what happens when those possibilities find a different purpose. Somewhere between convenience and escape, the question becomes: what are we giving up, and what are we so desperate to get away from?

That’s where it starts feeling like a modern-day Idiocracy. You laugh at the exaggeration, recognize pieces of your own world, then leave the theater and reach for your phone. The movie can point at the problem, but recognizing yourself in the joke doesn’t necessarily change anything. That’s a weird feeling to carry out of something this fun.

Not every piece lands. Some of the group gets much more attention than the rest, leaving other characters feeling less explored. The later stretch also pushes the silliness and drama further than it needs to. Still, the likable lead, surprising turns, and jokes worth catching keep it engaging.

Funny, strange, and full of ideas—an entertaining watch with an uncomfortable thought underneath it: we might already be living inside part of the punchline.

title: Whistle
review:
Whistle takes the classic “don’t touch that” horror setup and gives it a nasty hook: an ancient death whistle whose sound brings your future death looking for you. Curiosity gets the story moving. Figuring out how to survive the consequences is another problem entirely.

There’s something unsettling about that idea. Death isn’t a stranger picking victims at random—it’s something that already belongs to you, arriving before you’re ready. The threat turns the future into something immediate, making the question less about who’s coming and more about whether there’s any way to escape what’s yours.

The high-school setting adds a familiar pressure to the supernatural setup. A group of young people has to make sense of something far beyond their experience, with every unanswered question carrying a potentially ugly consequence. It’s a straightforward horror engine with a hook that doesn’t need much explaining.

The appeal is in that simplicity: a cursed object, a terrible sound, and the desperate search for a way to take back what’s been set in motion. Sometimes the scariest part of a bad decision is realizing that understanding it came too late.

title: In Cold Light
review:
In Cold Light builds its crime story around a frustrating idea: leaving prison doesn’t mean the life waiting outside has changed. Ava returns to a world where old ties still have power, and the possibility of moving forward quickly becomes a fight to stay alive.

The hook is the distance between freedom and a fresh start. Being outside is one thing. Finding a way beyond the people, choices, and damage that brought you there is another. That gives the familiar on-the-run setup a more personal question: what does escape actually look like when the past keeps coming with you?

Survival and family sit close together here. The danger isn’t only about getting away from whoever is chasing you; it’s also about facing the relationships that make leaving complicated. A way out can seem obvious from a distance. Living with everything attached to it is harder.

A modest crime thriller built around a recognizable struggle: wanting another chance while still caught in the world you already know. The premise carries more weight than the chase alone, even if the overall takeaway stays in solid, middle-ground territory.

title: Infinite Icon: A Visual Memoir
review:
Paris Hilton is one of those people you can recognize instantly and still know surprisingly little about. Infinite Icon approaches that gap through music, tracing the dreams, public scrutiny, and reinvention behind a very familiar face.

There’s something worth sitting with in that idea. When someone becomes a character in pop culture, it’s easy to forget they’re still a person building a life outside the version everyone thinks they know. Here, music becomes the thread connecting that public image to a more personal story.

The mix of performances and personal history makes this part concert film, part reflection on taking ownership of your narrative. The question underneath the glamour is more relatable than the celebrity: how do you keep moving forward when people have already decided who you are?

Our experience was mixed. There was appreciation for the story, but the emotional connection wasn’t equal—and one of us missed a chunk after falling asleep. That’s a limit on our experience, rather than proof that the movie drags. A 6/10 Wave reflects that split.

title: Send Help
review:
Getting stranded with your boss sounds like a nightmare before survival even enters the picture. Send Help takes that setup and finds something deliciously ugly inside it: the person used to calling the shots may have very little to offer when the office disappears.

There’s a satisfying tension in watching workplace authority meet a situation it can’t control. A title, money, and confidence only carry so much weight when staying alive depends on actual ability. Suddenly, being overlooked and being useless are two very different things.

That’s where the premise gets interesting. Two people need each other, but they also bring resentment, ego, and a history that doesn’t vanish just because they share a disaster. Cooperation sounds sensible. Trust is a much bigger ask.

The dark humor gives that conflict a nasty little edge. There’s room to enjoy the absurdity while still thinking about who holds power, who deserves it, and what happens when the balance changes. Surviving the island is one problem. Surviving each other is another.

This was a banger for both of us. A survival thriller with an ugly human problem at its center, and the kind of setup that makes “just work together” sound a whole lot easier than it is. An easy Wave recommendation.

title: Shelter
review:
Shelter starts with a man who has stepped away from the world, then gives him a reason he can’t stay there. Rescuing a young girl pulls him out of isolation and into danger, turning a quiet existence into a fight that reaches back into his past.

It’s a familiar action setup, but there’s a reason the protector story keeps coming around. The stakes are easy to understand: someone vulnerable needs help, and walking away would mean choosing your own safety over theirs. You don’t need a complicated explanation to understand why that matters.

The more interesting idea is what protection demands from someone who has made a life out of keeping his distance. Hiding might keep trouble away for a while, but it also means avoiding connection. Looking after another person forces that distance to close.

With Jason Statham at the center, the appeal is straightforward: danger, a reason to fight, and a character whose past won’t stay buried. The emotional hook gives the survival story something personal to hold onto, even when the territory feels familiar.

A solid middle-ground action pick. It doesn’t need to be a revelation to offer a reason to root for someone—and sometimes a clear purpose and someone worth protecting are enough.

title: Melania
review:
Melania follows the twenty days leading up to the 2025 presidential inauguration, but our biggest takeaway was how bizarre the whole experience felt. It’s a trippy watch—not because it’s a fantasy, but because this is an actual person’s life unfolding around an enormous public event.

There’s curiosity in that. You’re watching a world most people will never experience, and that alone gives you something to take in. But finding something interesting isn’t the same as loving the movie built around it. That’s where this landed for us: curious about what we were watching, without coming away particularly impressed.

The strangeness is what sticks. It’s a film we’d describe as an experience more readily than a recommendation—something that held our curiosity, but didn’t turn that curiosity into a stronger connection.

title: Dracula
review:
Dracula takes a story about a monster and puts a broken heart at its center. After losing his wife, a prince turns against God and becomes cursed with immortality. What follows is a search for the love he lost—and a reminder that living forever means very little when the person you want isn’t there.

That’s a strong foundation for this kind of movie. Love, grief, obsession, and horror all belong in the same room here. You can understand the longing without forgetting the danger attached to it. Wanting someone back is human. Building an eternity around that desire is where it becomes something else.

But our takeaway wasn’t just the tragedy. We had fun with this one. For a story carrying so much death and heartbreak, it was an entertaining watch that gave us plenty to enjoy. The romance gives the vampire story a personal reason to keep moving, while the darker side keeps that devotion from feeling entirely innocent.

There’s an interesting question underneath it all: when does holding on become refusing to let go? Dracula makes that question bigger, stranger, and bloodier than real life, but the feeling behind it is recognizable.

We both really liked it. A dark love story with an entertaining streak, and one that landed a little harder emotionally than it did critically. This one earned its place in the wave.

title: Cold Storage
review:
Cold Storage takes a deadly fungal outbreak and turns it into a very weird night at work. There’s something immediately uncomfortable about a threat that spreads before people fully understand what they’re dealing with. The pacing is where it stumbles. There are stretches that drag, and the energy doesn’t hold up consistently toward the end. For something with such a freaky premise, it has a few too many moments where your attention can drift.

Still, Cold Storage makes for a decent, low-pressure movie night. A little unsettling, a little stupid, and pretty easy to enjoy when you’re in the mood for that combination.

title: Obsession
status: reviewed
quote: Getting what you want has never felt this uncomfortable
brainReaction: Her performance keeps the discomfort compelling without overdoing it.
heartReaction: Trippy, toxic, and impossible to stop watching unfold.
review:
Obsession takes a romantic wish and follows it somewhere deeply uncomfortable. Wanting someone to love you sounds simple until the movie starts questioning what that love would look like without limits, distance, or a way to turn it off.

The acting is what makes it work. Inde Navarrette carries the heaviest material, making the situation unsettling without pushing it into something we wanted to turn away from. Michael Johnston helps sell the awkwardness on the other side. You believe the people enough to stay invested when everything around them starts feeling completely fucked.

What makes it especially trippy is how extreme behavior can still have something recognizable inside it. The movie stretches impatience, desperation, and the moments people lose control into a state somebody can’t easily escape. That’s disturbing to watch. So is the sense that a person is still in there, struggling against what’s happening.

The humor lands in that same uncomfortable space. It isn’t always trying to tell a joke; sometimes the situation is so awkward and wrong that laughing is the reaction that comes out. Then the horror hits, and the whole thing tightens again.

It keeps you curious about how this could possibly work out, without making the graphic moments feel overdone. Engaging, layered, and carried by performances that make the nightmare feel much too close.

title: Jackass: Best and Last

Jackass has always felt like a group of friends before it felt like a franchise. That’s what makes a final movie such a weird thing to watch. You can pass a name to somebody else. You can’t really replace this particular group of dudes or what it felt like watching them do their thing.

Best and Last leans heavily on familiar footage. If you’ve followed the movies and gone looking for their old clips, a lot of this will feel like something you’ve already seen. We went in expecting more new material, so there’s a real disappointment in realizing how much of the night is a highlight reel.

But the nostalgia carries a different kind of weight. Johnny Knoxville taking one more bow means something, even when the movie itself feels closer to a retrospective than a fresh chapter. The stunts might be repeat viewing; the feeling that this era is ending isn’t.

The theater experience made that even stranger. We expected a loud, obnoxious crowd movie. People laughed, but the exit was unexpectedly quiet, almost like leaving a funeral. There was something oddly respectful about it.

It’s a good throwback and a bittersweet farewell. Hard to judge purely as a new movie, easier to understand as a curtain call for people who helped shape a whole generation’s sense of stupid fun.

title: Disclosure Day
status: reviewed
quote: All the right pieces, without the payoff to match
brainReaction: A lot of buildup for a lackluster payoff.
heartReaction: Textbook Hollywood, with some trippy moments and familiar moves.
review:
Disclosure Day feels like a movie you could teach a film class around. Action, horror, comedy, carefully framed little routines: it has a bit of everything, placed where a big Hollywood story is supposed to put it. The question is whether that structure makes it satisfying.

We liked it more than we expected to, but there’s something strangely textbook about the experience. The camera follows small actions, shifts perspectives, and keeps showing you the machinery of a scene. At times it brings back the feeling of familiar Spielberg adventures and thrillers. At others, it feels like the movie is checking boxes.

The buildup is the bigger problem. It keeps you curious about what’s happening, then the eventual explanation doesn’t deliver enough to justify how long the movie has been winding you up. There’s a lot of anticipation for a payoff that feels pretty lackluster.

Some of the tricks are neat, and there are trippy moments worth leaning into. But the loose ends and the length leave too much of the work with the audience. Being asked to think about a movie is one thing; having to fill in what it leaves behind is another.

It’s a decent, sometimes cheesy watch that benefits from a big screen and a good sound system. You can recognize the craft without feeling the whole thing fully come alive. A respectable set of movie ingredients that needed a stronger finish.

There's something satisfying about a movie that lets conversation do the damage. The night keeps changing shape as attraction, insecurity, and frustration share the table. Funny, uncomfortable, and emotionally messy in a way that makes the whole setup worth sitting through.

title: You Can See Everything
status: reviewed
quote: Seeing everything doesn't mean you know what to believe

review:

A camera can show you a person all day and still leave the hardest question unanswered: what are you actually seeing?

That's where the movie gets its grip. A documentary subject is also somebody aware of being watched, while the people holding the camera have their own expectations. Every attempt to understand the situation becomes part of it. The awkwardness, the absurdity, and the uncertainty feed the same experience.

It's the kind of film that makes the act of watching feel active. You're considering the person, the presentation, and your own willingness to believe a story all at once. Fascinating, uncomfortable, and much harder to put into a neat box than the premise suggests. One of the strongest watches in this run.

There’s something uncomfortable about finding yourself sympathizing with someone you know you shouldn’t be rooting for. Wild Horse Nine makes that discomfort part of the experience, giving a criminal enough humanity to complicate an easy judgment.

The humor helps. It lets the film be entertaining while leaving room for something touching and thought-provoking underneath. You can recognize the person without forgetting the reasons you were hesitant to care about them in the first place.

That shifting perspective is what makes it interesting. Sympathy doesn’t have to mean approval, and understanding someone doesn’t erase what they’ve done. Sometimes a film works by making that distinction harder to sit with.

A good, interesting watch with humor, feeling, and a little moral discomfort to take home.

title: Wicker
status: reviewed
quote: What happens when someone doesn’t know the rules everyone else lives by?
brainReaction: A strange fantasy with an interesting social perspective.
heartReaction: Trippy, thought-provoking, and full of consequences.
review:
Wicker drops that question into a strange fantasy world and lets it ripple outward. Someone arrives without the assumptions and expectations that everyone around them has learned to take for granted. What feels normal to society suddenly looks different through a perspective that hasn’t been shaped by it.

The interesting part is that the influence goes both ways. Society starts shaping the outsider, but the outsider also changes the people around them. Their reactions and decisions reveal how much of what we accept comes from what we’ve been taught—and how unsettling it can be when someone doesn’t follow along.

That gives the film something to sit with beyond its trippy premise. Choices have consequences, and what people decide to protect, demand, or change can come at a cost.

An unusual, thought-provoking watch about the rules we inherit and what happens when someone enters the world without them.

title: Ebenezer
status: reviewed
quote: The scariest thing in the room might be the life you’ve built
brainReaction: A familiar story with questions about consequence and change.
heartReaction: A reminder that a second chance still needs a choice.
review:
A Christmas Carol has always had a ghost story underneath the holiday tradition. Ti West’s Ebenezer brings that idea forward: a man is forced to face his past, his present, and the future he’s creating through the way he treats other people.

The supernatural setup gives the story its spectacle, but the question at its center stays painfully human. What happens when the habits that made you feel secure have also left you alone? Scrooge can protect his money, his routines, and his pride, but none of those things can answer for the life passing him by.

There’s a reason this story keeps returning. Regret is recognizable, and the possibility of changing before it’s too late still has something to offer. The ghosts make a dramatic entrance; the harder part is what someone chooses to do after they leave.

A familiar seasonal story with room for a darker mood and a little reflection.
